items.title: Holo Player
items.text:
Firmware for the Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-1.28, driving a droid's holoprojector: it plays Motion-JPEG clips and shows images — animated GIFs included — on a 240×240 round panel, lights a NeoPixel ring, and aims two servos the way a dome's basic holoprojectors move. Everything is driven from a console on the board's USB-C port.

The board is an ESP32-S3R2 with 2 MB of PSRAM and 16 MB of flash, carrying a GC9A01 round IPS panel, a CST816S touch controller and a QMI8658 IMU. Clips live on an 11 MB LittleFS volume and go onto the board over the same serial console, as does new firmware.

  • Install

    From the browser in a few clicks, with esptool, or built from source. Update in place, or start fresh.

  • The board

    Pins, the P2 expansion header, and what is wired to what.

  • Play a clip

    Make a Motion-JPEG file, put it on the board, and play it.

  • Show an image

    A PNG, JPEG or GIF on the panel, where it stays until something replaces it. Animated GIFs play.

  • Wire the LED ring

    Three wires, and the power budget that decides whether it needs its own supply.

  • Aim the holoprojector

    The motions, and calibrating each axis' travel.

  • The board in the browser

    Put clips and images on the board, and try every command, from Chrome or Edge. No tools to install.

  • Console commands

    Every command the firmware registers.

The screen is off whenever nothing is showing

At boot, after screen clear, and when a clip ends, the panel is asleep with its backlight off — not black, but unpowered. That is deliberate, and it is why the first frame of a clip is never drawn to a dark screen. A colour or an image stays up until something replaces it.

items.title: Changelog
items.text:
Notable changes to the holo player firmware. The format follows Keep a Changelog and versions follow semantic versioning.

The version is not written down anywhere in the source. ESP-IDF derives it from git describe, so the release tag is the version baked into the image and reported by version and ota. See RELEASING.md.

items.title: Changed
items.text: • The CAN controller wrapper, libcanard and the Cyphal node are the kit's (canbus, libcanard and cyphal in external/esp-console-kit, shared with the dome panel's firmware), and this repository's copies of them are gone, with the external/libcanard and external/public_regulated_data_types submodules (now the kit's third_party/). Nothing the board does changed: the Kconfig values and the node's code are the same (the kit's can gained an optional print hook, a NULL check on its pin callback and Kconfig symbols for its task, defaulting to this board's values), and the image is 112 bytes larger. The holo's own Cyphal types (r2/holo/, with the port table) moved to main/dsdl/; tools/gen_dsdl.py generates only those, and checks the kit's DSDL revision; tools/can_check.py loads the kit's; make unit-test builds the kit's node tests against the holo's port table. Clone with --recursive.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• can: plain CAN frames on the host link's pins A and B, for checking a CAN transceiver and a bus before anything runs on it. can start takes the pins (1 Mbit/s unless -b; --listen never drives the bus, --selftest hears its own frames with no second node), can send sends one frame, can dump prints what arrives, can echo sends each frame back on the next ID, and can alone shows the bus's state, its error counters and the frames sent, received and dropped. can recover brings the controller back from bus-off; can stop gives the pins back. It refuses to start while the host link runs on those pins, and gpio refuses them while it runs. Documented in the manual's The board on Cyphal, "Testing the wiring".
  • tools/can_check.py, the computer's side, through a gs_usb adapter (candleLight, CANable): listen, send, flood, and echo, which sends numbered frames to a board running can echo on and checks that every one comes back, in order. flush empties the adapter after a python-can session, so that the next program to open it (cyphal_service) doesn't stall on a frame left for the computer.
  • A Cyphal node on CAN. link mode can (and a restart) hands the host link's pins A and B to it. It gets its node-ID by plug-and-play (uavcan.pnp.NodeIDAllocationData.1.0, from any allocator on the bus, asked for again at every start and never saved) or from a fixed setting. It sends uavcan.node.Heartbeat once a second and answers uavcan.node.GetInfo with its name (r2.dome.holo.front unless changed), the firmware's version and commit, and a unique ID made from the chip's factory MAC address, so that an allocator gives the same node-ID across reflashes and settings wipes. With a fixed node-ID it listens 2 s for another node with it before going online; with plug-and-play it listens at least 1 s from its start (a heartbeat's longest period) before taking up an allocated node-ID, and doesn't if another node was heard on it in that time or in the last 3 s; and if it ever hears its node-ID from another node it stops sending, with one warning, until told to start again. The board keeps acknowledging the bus throughout. Documented in the manual's The board on Cyphal and Host link: CAN.
  • cyphal: the node's state, node-ID, name, unique ID and plug-and-play pseudo-ID, the bus and its counters; cyphal id (a fixed node-ID, or auto for plug-and-play), cyphal name and cyphal bitrate (saved, and in a configuration backup), cyphal restart and cyphal reset.
  • Bus-off: the node brings the controller back by itself, within a second; when bus-offs come back to back (a board that can't see its own bits on the bus: a silent transceiver, or VIO, RXD or TXD not connected), it waits 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and then 30 s between recoveries until the bus has stayed up for a minute, and logs the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 8th, ... bus-off in a row, not one a second. cyphal shows the wait. The bus's state in can and cyphal is read from the error counters beside it (error-warning at 96, error-passive at 128); bus errors counts every error but lost arbitration, CRC errors on received frames included; and can send while bus-off, or can recover when not, refuses without an error line from the driver.
  • libcanard v4.0.0 (external/libcanard) and the DSDL (external/public_regulated_data_types) as submodules. A build needs libcanard (git submodule update --init); the DSDL is needed only by tools/gen_dsdl.py and the hardware tests. The C headers for the data types are generated by tools/gen_dsdl.py (Nunavut) and committed, so the build needs no Python packages.
  • Tests: make unit-test builds the node's unique ID, pseudo-ID, name rules, parsing and plug-and-play's request, reply, timing and in-use check with the computer's compiler; make can-test runs the hardware tests in tests/hardware/ (pytest and pycyphal, through a gs_usb adapter, with pycyphal's allocator for plug-and-play; make can-setup makes their venv). The unit tests also cover the holo's Cyphal conversions (requests, Status's parts, Event, the file services' paths and errors, MediaInfo, the calibration registers' values), and the hardware tests the holo's ports (motions, light, setpoints, scenes, screen, ring, events, the lists against the HTTP API, the calibration registers, a clip under load), with a soak, test_soak.py, run with --soak-minutes.
  • The Cyphal node is managed the standard way. Its settings are registers (uavcan.register.Access and List): uavcan.node.id, r2.node.name and uavcan.can.bitrate, the same saved settings as cyphal id, name and bitrate, and a pair for each of the holo's eleven ports, uavcan.pub.status.id and so on (the port number, saved, 65535 for off) and uavcan.pub.status.type (its type, read-only), with the defaults of r2_cyphal_dsdl's port table. A write is checked, saved and applies from the node's next start; one the board can't take leaves the register as it was, a port number another port has (the node's own included) among them. uavcan.node.ExecuteCommand restarts the board, resets it to the factory settings, all or nothing (the node's registers, touch reporting and the board's settings, keeping the scenes, files, servo calibration and drive policy, network and host link), identifies it (the ring blinks white and the screen shows the crosshair for 5 s, then both go back) or stores (nothing to do); other commands are refused. uavcan.node.port.List goes out every 10 s, with the ports the node really has. Documented in the manual's The board on Cyphal and Cyphal interface.
  • The holo on Cyphal (r2.holo.*): Motion (service 100) starts any motion with every parameter, through the code the HTTP API's POST /holo/motion runs, so it is refused in the same words; its off lets the servos go limp and turns the ring off. Light (service 101) is the holo's light on the LED ring: off, on, pulse, flicker, blink at a level and a period, an optional colour, a time limit after which the ring goes back to what it was doing, and leia (a timed flicker at full and the holo to the centre, which answers whether the centre ran). Axes subscribed (subject 2303) is a stream of setpoints, each a direct move with no easing that stops the motion running; Axes published (2302) is where the board has put the axes, ten times a second while they move and once a second at rest. Status (2300) is the holo's motion and readiness, the last motion asked for, both axes, the ring with its timed mode, the screen (what shows, a clip's progress, the backlight) and the scene running to its end, within 250 ms of a change and once a second. The heartbeat's health is advisory while the holo can't move. cyphal counts the holo's requests and setpoints, and each port's messages queued for the bus with those a newer one replaced before they were.
  • The board's own features on Cyphal: Scene (service 102) applies a saved scene by its slot or its name, or ends the one running, through the code POST /scenes/apply and /scenes/end run; Screen (103) shows a clip, an image, a colour, the crosshair or nothing and sets the backlight, through POST /screen/show's, DELETE /screen's and PATCH /screen's; Ring (104) sets the LED ring as PATCH /leds does. Each is refused as the HTTP API refuses it, in the same words. Event (subject 2301) carries every clip and scene starting and ending, and touches while touch reporting is on, with the board's own sequence number, from the record the HTTP API's events come from: two at once both go, in order, and none is lost while that record still has it. Scene and Screen requests, and identify, are carried out one at a time by a second worker task (7.5 KB stack), so that a still being decoded never holds up the setpoints or Status. cyphal shows that worker, Event's queue, and the most frames the transmit queue has held. Documented in the manual's The board on Cyphal and Cyphal interface.
  • The lists and the calibration on Cyphal: ListScenes (service 105) gives the saved scenes one a call with their slots, as GET /scenes lists them; the standard uavcan.file.List (406) and uavcan.file.GetInfo (405) give the board's files, as fs ls sees them (a directory's entries by index in name order, directories marked with a /; each one's size and time, read-only; with the board busy, List isn't answered, since its empty name would end a listing, and the client asks again); MediaInfo (106) describes a clip or an image from its header, through the lookup GET /media/info runs, and says whether the screen can show it and why not. The file services and MediaInfo run on the node's second worker, so that an upload holding the storage volume never holds up the setpoints. The holo's registers: r2.holo.horizontal.endpoints_us and r2.holo.vertical.endpoints_us (closed and open, 0 0 to clear), ….release and ….settle_ms (the drive policy), over the servos' own saved values, the ones holo endpoints, the web app's calibration and PUT /servos/policy change, written and read at once (by the node's worker); and r2.touch.reporting, the board's touch setting. Documented in the manual's The board on Cyphal and Cyphal interface.
  • The LED ring pulses and blinks, and has the holo light's level and timed modes: leds pulse and leds blink with -p <ms>; -l <pct> (a share of the brightness) on every mode but off, and -t <s> (then back to what it was doing) on colour, off, flicker, pulse and blink. A timed mode and a blink no longer wake the board 50 to 100 times a second, and the ring's task is made once and kept. The web app's status card shows a level other than 100 and counts a timed mode's time left down. PATCH /api/v1/leds and a scene's leds take pulse, blink, period_ms, level and time_s; GET /api/v1/leds reports period_ms, level, a timed mode (timed: its time left and what follows) and leia. The host link's LEDS frame takes modes 5 (pulse) and 6 (blink) with an optional period after its flags, and the status block reports them. The web app's Show and Scenes pages offer pulse and blink, and the scene editor a pulse's or a blink's period, the level and a time. A scene that restores the ring puts back a timed mode for the rest of its time.
  • cyphal register [<name> [<value>…]]: the same registers on the console, listed, read or written with the same checks. cyphal shows the services' counters and the worker that does their waiting (a register's write to flash, a restart, identify), so that the node's own task never waits.
  • r2_cyphal_dsdl (external/r2_cyphal_dsdl, the holo's own Cyphal types and port table) as a submodule; tools/gen_dsdl.py generates the C headers from it and the standard types together, and the port defaults from its port table.
  • tools/yakut_can.py (make yakut): Yakut on the board through a gs_usb adapter on macOS, opening and closing the adapter only while the board is quiet; registers only (it refuses execute-command, by every name Yakut's click version gives it, and calls to ExecuteCommand, during which a candleLight stopped passing frames on the bench, and what would leave the board never quiet as the adapter closes).

items.title: Changed
items.text:
• The host link on CAN (link mode can): link shows the pins and who has them ("for the Cyphal node"), and leaves out the protocol, baud rate, address, groups, events and counters, which CAN doesn't use; they stay saved for UART and RS485, and the console says so when one is changed. The web app's Host link card hides them while CAN is chosen. GET /api/v1/link is unchanged, and its description says which fields CAN ignores.
  • gpio names what holds a host link pin: host link UART TX, host link RS485 DE, or "CAN TX, for the Cyphal node", in place of host link (A). They are reserved from the moment the transport has started, and not at all if it failed to start: link then says off: can didn't start (...). A Cyphal node whose start failed is restarted only with the board (cyphal restart says so), since it no longer has the pins.
  • can refuses to start, stop, send, recover, dump or echo while the Cyphal node holds the controller; can alone still reports the bus. Before, can stop stopped the controller whoever had started it.
  • The manual's Run buttons ask before running a link command that changes a setting (link mode, pins, reset, proto, address, groups, events).
  • The CAN controller's sample point is 85 % of the bit, not the 87.5 % asked for: IDF 6.1's timing on the ESP32-S3 gives 20 time quanta at every bitrate, and 87.5 % is out of the controller's reach at 1 Mbit/s. The manual says so.
  • cyphal reset puts the port numbers back to their defaults too.
  • Looking at a clip's or an image's header (GET /media/info, Cyphal's MediaInfo, and the check before one is shown) takes its memory from PSRAM first: the GIF decoder's 24 KB, a clip's frame tables, a JPEG's bytes and libpng's state, up to 29 KB of internal RAM before, 4 to 9 KB now, which a playing clip's frames need. Playback itself is unchanged.
  • Touch reporting is one of the board's settings: GET /api/v1/settings has touch.reporting, PATCH sets it (and turns touch on or off now), DELETE puts it back to its default, the console's settings shows it and settings touch on|off sets it, the web app's Settings page has a switch for it, and the Cyphal register r2.touch.reporting is the same setting. The board starts with touch reporting on if it says so, CONFIG_BOARD_TOUCH_AUTOSTART being only its default; touch on and touch off still change it until the next start without saving. It is in a configuration backup (NVS holo_cfg, touch).
  • The Cyphal node's libcanard heap is 32 KB of PSRAM (was 16 KB), its transmit queue 160 frames (was 64) and its task's stack 3 KB (was 2.5 KB); a worker task with a 4.5 KB stack joins it at its first start.
  • A message the Cyphal node publishes waits in its mailbox until the transmit queue has room for the whole of it, rather than being dropped.
  • The hardware tests' console answers linenoise's terminal queries even when one arrives split between two reads of the port; one that went unanswered left the console with no prompt (seen three times in the tests).
  • leds shows a pulse's or a blink's period, a level other than 100, and a timed mode's time left and what follows. leds rainbow keeps the ring's colour for the next mode that has one, rather than forgetting it.
  • GET /api/v1/events (the kept happenings as JSON) is sent in chunks straight from the stored happenings, rather than parsed back into one tree and printed whole: at most a few KB of internal RAM where it took 16-18 KB with all 32 kept, which set the board's low-water mark while a clip played and the web app polled. The body is byte for byte the same; the reply has Transfer-Encoding: chunked in place of a Content-Length. (esp-console-kit b8d24e2.) A reader that stalls while happenings are made now has its connection closed, never a reply with one missing (59f2670, on the kit's main).
  • The video player's task is made once, at start, and waits between plays, rather than being made for every clip, GIF and scene restore: its stack, now 4.5 KB (8 KB before; 1.8 KB is the least it was seen to leave free, in rapid replacement), is held for good, about 5 KB less internal RAM free at rest, and is no longer taken at each start, where it could be refused. A stop now also cuts short the wait for a GIF's next frame. Any show (a clip, an image or GIF, a colour, the calibration pattern) that finds the last playback still not stopped after 2 s is refused, with what was playing did not stop within 2 s over HTTP and Cyphal: nothing is drawn, the stop stands and the screen goes dark at once. Before, a clip would have started alongside it, and a colour or a still was drawn and then put out by the old playback's end.
  • A GIF takes its memory only once what was playing has stopped: image show and POST /screen/show check it first, as before, but open it (its 24 KB decoder and its two DMA paint buffers) after the panel is taken, the paint buffers first. The cost: running out of memory now comes after the show is accepted, and ends the animation at once (clip_ended with finished: false, the screen dark, the reason on the console).
  • esp-console-kit moved to its main (2311a74): radio and MAC handling for the dome panel's ESP32-P4, and CMD_I2C_DEFAULT_PORT; nothing changes on this board.

items.title: Fixed
items.text:
• A timed scene past its time, in the moment before it ends, read as one with no duration: GET /scenes's remaining_s null, the host link's status block 0xFFFF, now 0.
  • GET /screen could catch a clip that had just started half-recorded (no path, 0 frames). The player's record is now copied under a lock of its own, never held for longer than the copy.
  • Touch could be started or stopped from two places at once (the console and the Cyphal register, or the settings over HTTP), making two drivers or deleting one under its task: start and stop now take turns.
  • A 240-pixel-wide animated GIF shown over a playing clip or GIF was always refused (it could not be drawn): it was opened before the playback it replaced had given back its memory. See Changed.
  • A clip or GIF that failed after it was accepted (the file not opened, no memory for its buffers, a broken GIF frame) was reported as played out: clip_ended said finished: true, and a scene that ends with its clip ran its then at once. Now finished: false, and the panel sleeps rather than keep what the failed clip replaced.
  • A clip or GIF that ended at once could have its clip_ended sent before its clip_started. The start is now told before the player has the clip.
  • A scene that ends with its clip could miss that end and run on until another scene or POST /scenes/end: a clip that failed or played out within moments of being shown had its end thrown away with those of the playback the scene replaced, and a scene showing the clip it replaced could be ended at once by the old playback's end. The scene now knows its own clip's playback, and a clip that fails ends its scene by: replaced, without its then. A scene's time running out as another scene is applied no longer lets its then put things back over the new scene. A colour or the calibration pattern refused because the playback before it did not stop now says so, rather than the panel did not take it.

The board's settings can now be backed up to a small text file and restored, a backup never holding a Wi-Fi network or password; the board can be told not to rejoin its network at start; and an ESP-IDF 6.1 I2C driver bug that could corrupt memory after a timed-out read is patched.

A board on 1.0.x updates from the Install page (which keeps settings and clips), over Wi-Fi from the web app, or with ota put over the console.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• Backing up the settings. nvs_export writes everything the board remembers -- scenes, start-up settings, servo calibration, the host link, the web app's name and allowed sites -- as one small text file, and nvs_import restores it: from the board's backup/ directory, a URL, or the console. The whole file is checked before anything is written, the configuration as it was is saved first, and only what differs is written. A backup never holds a Wi-Fi network, the access point's passphrase or the web password, so it is safe to keep and share; nvs_inventory shows what is in and why anything is not. Documented in the manual's Backing up the settings.
  • wifi auto [on|off]: whether the board rejoins its network when it starts. Off, it keeps the network but stays off it until asked (wifi on, a join, or BOOT), and the access point only comes on by itself at start when there is no network to rejoin.

items.title: Changed
items.text: • When a motion is cut short because an axis refused it, holo's status now says which motion, how long ago and, when one axis refused it, which -- ; <motion> stopped <n> s ago: <reason> (<axis>) -- where it said only ; stopped: <reason>. The manual's holo page now has a sample status and what each line means.

items.title: Fixed
items.text:
• An I2C read that timed out could make the next probe of the bus -- the IMU's at start, i2cdetect, a servo board's attach -- write a few bytes through a stale pointer in ESP-IDF 6.1's I2C driver, corrupting memory somewhere at random. Every probe and read now goes through a guard that clears that state first. (esp-console-kit's i2c_bus_guard, found on the dome panel, where it caused panics.)
  • Forgetting a network whose join had failed -- on the console, the Network page or DELETE /api/v1/network/known -- now stops the board retrying it. Before, it went on trying the forgotten network in the background every 30 seconds. (esp-console-kit a535a49.)

Everything the console does can now be done over Wi-Fi: a web app on your network, or on the board's own access point, handles updates, files, the screen, the LEDs, the holo and scenes, all through an HTTP API that scripts can use too. A controller on a wire can run the board over UART or RS485, and both hear what happens as it happens.

A board on 1.0.0 updates from the Install page (which keeps settings and clips) or with ota put over the console. From this release on, updates can also come over Wi-Fi.

items.title: The board over Wi-Fi
items.text:
• A web app, for phones and computers, at http://holo-xxxx.local/ or the board's address (web on the console prints both):
  • Status: what's showing, the firmware, the network, and whether a newer release is out;
  • Show: play any clip or show any image on the board, a colour or the alignment crosshair, the backlight, and the LEDs' pattern, colour and brightness;
  • Holo: point the holo on a drag pad, start a behaviour, and calibrate each servo;
  • Scenes: save the screen, LEDs and holo together, apply one with a tap, and choose the one the board starts with;
  • Files: browse the board's storage, upload several files with progress, rename, move, copy, download and delete;
  • Settings, Network and Update.

On a phone, Status, Show, Holo and Scenes are tabs and the rest are under More. Documented in The board over Wi-Fi. - Updates over Wi-Fi. Upload a .bin (checked before it is written: a downgrade or another project's file is flagged), or have the board fetch the latest release itself, checked against the release's SHA-256. It streams into the slot that isn't running, so a broken image never becomes the boot image; the other slot stays one tap away. Also ota pull <url|channel> and ota activate [slot] on the console. Documented in Updating the firmware. - An HTTP API under /api/v1, which the web app is built on: files, the screen and media, the LEDs, the holo and servos, scenes, settings, the network, the web server's settings, and firmware updates. It is described in OpenAPI 3.1, served by each board at /api/v1/openapi.json and browsable in the HTTP API explorer, with a guide and curl recipes. - Events, not polling. GET /api/v1/events is a stream of Server-Sent Events: the screen, LEDs, holo, running scene, scenes, settings, network and update session as each changes, and clip_started, clip_ended, scene_started, scene_ended and touch as they happen, numbered, with the last 32 replayed to a client that reconnects. While a clip plays or a scene runs, their state comes every 5 seconds too, to sync to. The web app follows it, so a change made anywhere (the console, a script, another browser, a host) shows on every open page at once. - The board's own access point. wifi ap on starts holo-xxxx at 192.168.4.1 (WPA2, with a random passphrase it keeps), and a phone that joins is offered the board's page. If the board can't join a network within 20 seconds of starting, the access point comes on by itself for 5 minutes. Pressing BOOT with the board off the network rejoins it, or turns the access point on for 5 minutes. Under "Wi-Fi fallback" in menuconfig. - Protection. Pages on other sites can't drive the board from your browser. An optional password (web password, or the Settings page) guards every change, downloads and the web settings. A short list of trusted sites -- Swagger Editor, and this project's documentation -- may call the API from a browser; web cors changes it.

items.title: Scenes
items.text:
• Scenes: what the screen shows, what the LEDs do and how the holo moves, saved together by name and applied in one call, with one chosen to run at every start. Up to 16.
  • Scenes that end: when their clip has played (once, or loops times) or after duration_s, and then (then) put everything back as it was -- a twitch twitches again -- or turn it all off. scene end or POST /api/v1/scenes/end ends one early.
  • Scene slots: a number from 1 to 255 a scene can be applied by, for small controllers (slot in the scene, scene slot on the console, or the scene editor).
  • Settings: the backlight, LED brightness and LED count the board starts with.
  • An LED flicker: the colour flickering like a failing hologram (leds flicker [<colour>]).

items.title: The host link
items.text:
• A controller on a wire -- an Arduino, an ESP32, a Raspberry Pi, a dome controller -- runs the board over UART, or RS485 through a transceiver, on P2's spare pins (GPIO21, 33 and 15).
  • JSON lines: the HTTP API one request a line (POST /scenes/apply {"name":"cantina"}, answered 200 {...}), with tags, and on RS485 an address on every request and groups that act together.
  • Native frames for small hosts: a few bytes with a CRC (SCENE 3, LEDS, HOLO, a 12-byte STATUS).
  • Events: pushed as they happen on UART, with no extra wire, or kept for the host to fetch, with a count of those waiting on every reply.

Set up with link on the console, PATCH /api/v1/link, or the Settings page. tools/hostlink.py talks to it from a computer. Documented in The host link, a wiring page for UART and RS485, and the protocol. I2C is described ahead of the firmware, to come.

items.title: The board in the browser
items.text:
• A documentation page that talks to the board over Web Serial (desktop Chrome, Edge or Opera), with nothing to install: a file manager for /data (drop to upload, drag to move, every transfer checked by SHA-256), every command the board lists grouped by what it's for, and the console.
  • Run buttons throughout the documentation: in those browsers, each board command in the pages has a ▶ that runs it on a connected board, output underneath. Commands that change something ask first. Connecting doesn't restart the board, and it works in the offline documentation too.

items.title: Console and tools
items.text:
• scene, settings, link, wifi scan, wifi ap, web (on|off, password, hostname, cors), ota pull and ota activate.
  • make api-smoke HOST=... calls a board's API, follows its event stream, and checks every reply against the OpenAPI description; make api-validate checks the description and its examples.

items.title: Changed
items.text:
• video play refuses a file it can't play at once, saying why, and leaves the screen alone. Before, it stopped what was showing and printed the reason from the player's task.
  • The console takes commands of up to 16 words. holo twitch -r 40 -i 1-3 -t 5 lost its last word.
  • Board output in the documentation is in text code blocks, and bare code blocks hold only board commands, which tools/check_command_docs.py checks, so every ▶ runs a real command.

items.title: Known issues
items.text:
• On macOS, fs_xfer.py put fails through Apple's driver (cu.usbmodem…): 1 KB XMODEM blocks arrive corrupted. Use cu.wchusbserial…. The browser's file manager switches to 128-byte blocks there instead.
  • RS485 has been tried through a plain UART adapter, but not yet on a bus with transceivers.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• Install from the browser. The Install page in each release's documentation flashes that release onto the board over Web Serial (desktop Chrome, Edge or Opera), with no toolchain. It reads the board first: on one running Holo Player with the same partition layout it updates, keeping settings and clips; on a blank board or other firmware it does a fresh install; and a complete overwrite is always available behind a confirmation. Images are checked against SHA-256 before writing and MD5 after, and the boot log confirms the result. The offline documentation zip carries the same installer and firmware, served on localhost by its serve.py with no internet. esptool and building from source stay documented for other browsers. Documented in Install.
  • Every image a blank board needs, on the Release. Besides the application, each Release now carries the bootloader, partition table and initial OTA data, so esptool can install a release without ESP-IDF.
  • GIFs, animated too. image show takes a GIF. A one-frame GIF is a still; an animated one plays on the video player's task — so video stop and video status work on it — looping as the file says and leaving its last frame up when it stops. Frames are composited onto a canvas and only what changed is painted, so a typical 240×240 GIF costs a few milliseconds a frame. The decoder is bitbank2/AnimatedGIF, a new submodule: in an existing clone, run git submodule update --init before building. Documented in Images.
  • Still images. image show <file> puts a PNG or a baseline 4:2:0 JPEG on the panel, centred, where it stays until something else takes the screen; image info <file> describes one without showing it. JPEG stills reuse the clip player's decoder, and PNG is libpng, streamed row by row into the same 16-line blocks — so no whole image is held except for interlaced files, which Adam7 makes impossible to read a row at a time. Nothing that fails disturbs the screen: the file, its format and its size are all checked before the panel is touched. Documented in Images.
  • Screen alignment. screen calibration (or screen calib) draws a centred crosshair with an up arrow at the crossing, for mounting the panel behind a dome's lens. The lines straddle the seam between pixels 119 and 120, so the crossing is the panel's true centre. Documented in Mounting the screen.
First tagged release. Everything below already worked; this is the point it became a version you can name, flash and report.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• Video. Motion-JPEG QuickTime playback on the round panel, on the clip's own timing, with video play|stop|status|info|verify. Frames decode 16 lines at a time into alternating DMA buffers so decoding and the SPI transfer overlap; a 240×240 clip runs at 30 fps with no late frames.
  • Screen. screen colour and screen clear. The panel sleeps with its backlight off whenever nothing is showing, and a clip's first frame is never drawn to a dark screen.
  • NeoPixel ring. leds with a solid colour, brightness, and the wipe and rainbow patterns, once or looped.
  • Holoprojector. Two servos on MCPWM as pan and tilt, driven by the shared holo engine: twitch, wag, nod, scan, circle, move, nudge, center. Endpoints calibrate with holo endpoints and persist in NVS under the pin, so they follow the wiring. Servos stay limp until the first move.
  • Board. GC9A01 LCD, CST816S touch and QMI8658 IMU on a shared I2C bus, with lcd, touch and imu.
  • Files and updates over the console. An 11 MB LittleFS volume at /data, fs for working with it, and ota put for installing firmware over the serial console when the board cannot be reached by USB. Both transfer over XMODEM-1K with SHA-256 verification; the host side is tools/fs_xfer.py in esp-console-kit.
  • Documentation site built from manual/, published per version.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text: The screen is dark and nothing seems wrong. That is the normal resting state. The panel sleeps with its backlight off whenever nothing is showing — at boot, after screen clear, and when a clip ends. Try screen colour red. A transparent PNG shows white where it should be transparent. It is not transparent any more — the panel has no alpha, so transparency is composited over black when the file is decoded. White means the transparent pixels really are white in the file, with the alpha channel hiding them. Export with the background you want (details). A JPEG that opens everywhere else will not show on the board. The decoder reads baseline 4:2:0 only. only baseline JPEG is supported means the file is progressive; unsupported colour sampling means it is 4:4:4, which is what ffmpeg writes by default from a still RGB image; bad JPEG data on a file that is not corrupt means 4:2:2. All three re-encode the same way: ffmpeg -i in.jpg -c:v mjpeg -q:v 3 -pix_fmt yuvj420p out.jpg (details). A PNG avoids the question entirely. image show refuses a picture that looks the right shape. It is larger than 240×240. Images are not scaled or cropped to fit — the framing stays yours — so resize it on the host first (details). A GIF plays slower than it does in a browser. If its frames ask for 10 ms or less, the board shows each for 100 ms — but so do Chrome and Firefox, so check it in one of those rather than an image viewer. Otherwise video status while it plays will show frames running late: it changes too much of a 240×240 panel per frame. The ceiling is about 22 fps when every pixel changes; lower its frame rate or its size (details). image: … truncated: it ends before the GIF trailer. The file was cut short, almost always in transfer. Send it again with fs_xfer.py put, which verifies what arrives (details). Every LED shows white, whatever colour I send — including leds off. The data rate is set to 400 kHz, which is for WS2811 strips. A WS2812 reads a 400 kHz "0" as a "1", so every frame comes out white, including the one meant to turn the strip off. Set 800 kHz in menuconfig (details). The first LED flickers or shows the wrong colour; the rest are fine. A 3.3 V data line into a 5 V-powered strip, which is marginal by design. Add a 74AHCT1G125 buffer powered from the strip's +5 V between GPIO16 and DIN (details). The board resets or browns out when the servos move. Servo power is coming from the board. A small servo draws 0.5–1 A starting or stalling. Give the servos their own 5 V supply and share only ground (details). holo wag nods instead of shaking its head. The two servos are swapped relative to the default. Change Which servo pans in menuconfig rather than rewiring (details). One axis moves the wrong way. Save its endpoints reversed — closed above open turns an axis round: holo endpoints v 1950 1300 (details). The servos are limp and ignore me. They are limp until the first move, and after holo off or servo_off all. Any motion command drives them again. holo led does nothing. There is no light on this board. The holo is registered with its light unset, so holo led and the light half of holo leia have nothing to drive. The NeoPixel ring is separate, and is driven by leds. A 240×240 clip stutters, but a 120×120 one is fine. Check the dimensions are both multiples of 8. If they are not, the player falls back to decoding whole frames, which roughly doubles the per-frame cost at 240×240 (details). Playback is occasionally late for no obvious reason. Something wrote to flash. A flash write pauses both cores while the cache is off, which can make a frame late. Saving a Wi-Fi network mid-clip will do it (details). fs_xfer.py hangs, or the console does not answer. idf.py monitor is still holding the serial port. Only one program can have it at a time. Downloads from the board are corrupt, but uploads are fine. On macOS, WCH's CH34x driver loses data coming from the board above 230400 baud, whatever the block size. That is why downloads default to 230400. Try a lower --get-baud (details). i2cdetect does not show the touch controller at 0x15. A CST816S only answers on I2C while the screen is being touched. Hold a finger on the glass and run it again. imu id reports an unexpected address. The QMI8658's SA0 is tied low, but Waveshare's own headers disagree about which address that gives, so both 0x6B and 0x6A are probed. Either is normal. version reports a commit hash instead of a version number. The firmware was built from an untagged commit, which is what a development build looks like. A -dirty suffix means there were uncommitted changes. Release builds report their tag (details). An update over serial finished, but the board still runs the old firmware. If the new image was installed with ota put -n it was made the boot image without restarting. Otherwise, a reset before the new image confirmed itself rolls back to the previous one by design (details). Installing over USB put back an old version. The browser installer, esptool and idf.py flash all write ota_0 and boot it, whichever slot the console-installed firmware was using. The Install page says the browser can't talk to serial ports. Web Serial is only in desktop Chrome, Edge and Opera — not Firefox, Safari, or any phone. Use one of those, or install with esptool (details). The Install page says there is no firmware to install. Only a release's documentation carries firmware; the development version (dev) and previews do not. Switch to a release with the version selector at the top of the page. Opened from the documentation zip, the Install page says the installer can't run. Browsers won't use a serial port from a page opened as a file. Run python3 serve.py in the unzipped folder; it serves the pages on localhost with no internet needed (details). The browser lists no serial port for the board. Try another USB-C cable — some carry only power. On Windows and older macOS, the CH343P needs WCH's driver. The board appears as cu.wchusbserial… or cu.usbmodem… on macOS and as USB-SERIAL CH343 on Windows. The installer says the port is in use. Another program has it: idf.py monitor, a serial terminal, fs_xfer.py, or another browser tab. Close it and connect again. The installer says the board didn't answer. Its reset into the bootloader didn't take. Hold BOOT, tap RESET, let go of BOOT, and connect again. Writing fails part way through. Install again; the board may not start until an install completes. If it keeps failing, lower the baud rate under Advanced, and avoid USB hubs. The installer won't offer to update: the partition layout changed. The release divides the flash up differently from the firmware on the board, so the settings and clips it would keep could be misread. Copy off anything you want to keep with fs_xfer.py, install with Complete overwrite, and put them back. A ▶ or the Board page says the port is in use. One program at a time: close idf.py monitor, any serial terminal and fs_xfer.py. The Install page counts too, and so does another browser tab. The connection follows you from page to page within one tab, but two tabs can't share it (details). The Board page says the board didn't answer at its console. It isn't running Holo Player: it is blank, held in its bootloader, or running something else. Press RESET and connect again. A blank board needs installing first. An upload through the browser is slow, or seems stuck. About 7 KB/s is normal, so a 1.9 MB clip takes four to five minutes. Keep the tab in front, because browsers slow down background tabs. Cancel an upload that stops moving: the board keeps nothing from an upload that doesn't finish, so send it again (details). holo-xxxx.local doesn't open. Some Android phones and some networks don't resolve .local names. Use the board's address instead: web on the console prints it, and your router's device list shows it too, under the same name. The board must be on the same network as you: wifi says which network it joined (details). The web app lost the board after an update, on its access point. The access point is off after every restart, including the one that finishes an update, unless the board can't join a network then. Press BOOT (the access point comes on for 5 minutes if the board still can't join its network), or run wifi ap on on the console, and join holo-xxxx again. The access point went away after a few minutes. One that came on by itself at start, or from the BOOT button, turns off after 5 minutes. Press BOOT for another 5, or keep it on: the Network page's switch, or wifi ap on. An update over Wi-Fi says "another update is in progress". One update at a time, whoever started it: another tab, a script, or ota put on the console. The Update page shows it and can cancel it. curl -X DELETE http://holo-xxxx.local/api/v1/ota/image does the same. Changes over the web ask for a password. Someone set one with web password. Ask them, or clear it on the console with web password --clear.

items.title: The board
items.text:
The Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-1.28 (Rev3) is an ESP32-S3R2 with 2 MB of quad PSRAM in the package and 16 MB of flash, carrying a round display, a touch controller, an IMU and a battery charger on a 1.28-inch disc.

Pin assignments below come from the Rev3 schematic netlist; Waveshare's own documentation, TFT_eSPI Setup302 and the NuttX esp32s3-ws-lcd128 board agree with them. They are defined in components/board_ws128/include/board.h, which is the authority if the two ever disagree.

items.title: What is on the board
items.text: Part Detail Display GC9A01A, 240×240 round IPS, 4-wire SPI on SPI2 Touch CST816S, I2C address 0x15 IMU QMI8658A, I2C address 0x6B (or 0x6A) Battery Sensed on ADC1 channel 0 through a 200 kΩ/100 kΩ divider, so Vbat = 3 × Vadc USB USB-C through a CH343P bridge to UART0

items.title: Display
items.text:
Signal GPIO SCLK 10 MOSI 11 MISO 12 (routed to the panel, unused) CS 9 DC 8 RST 14 Backlight 2

The backlight pin drives an N-FET and is active high with a pull-down, so the backlight is off at reset and stays off until the firmware turns it on.

The visible area is circular, and its centre falls between pixels 119 and 120 on both axes. screen calibration draws a crosshair on that centre for aligning the panel in a dome — see Mounting the screen.

GPIO10 is not SPI2's IOMUX clock pin, so the signals go through the GPIO matrix. On the S3 that limits reads rather than writes, and the panel is only ever written to, so it costs nothing here.

items.title: I2C bus
items.text:
One bus is shared by the touch controller and the IMU.

Signal GPIO SDA 6 SCL 7

It runs at 400 kHz. There are no pull-up resistors on the board, which matters if you hang anything else off the bus. i2cdetect will show what is answering.

The touch controller is an awkward bus citizen: a CST816S only answers on I2C while the screen is being touched. That is why reading its ID at startup is disabled (CONFIG_ESP_LCD_TOUCH_CST816S_DISABLE_READ_ID), and why i2cdetect will usually not show 0x15 unless you are touching the glass as it runs.

Device Address INT RST CST816S touch 0x15 5 13 QMI8658A IMU 0x6B, or 0x6A 4 (INT1), 3 (INT2) —

The IMU's SA0 pin is tied low, but Waveshare's own headers disagree about which address that produces, so the firmware probes both. imu id reports which one answered.

items.title: P2 expansion header
items.text:
P2 is the 12-pin, 1.0 mm-pitch SH connector on the back of the board, and the only place to connect anything.

Pin Signal Pin Signal 1 GND 7 GPIO15 2 VSYS 8 GPIO16 3 RUN (reset) 9 GPIO17 4 BOOT (GPIO0) 10 GPIO18 5 GND 11 GPIO21 6 3V3 12 GPIO33

Six GPIOs are free for your own use: 15, 16, 17, 18, 21 and 33. This firmware already claims three of them — GPIO16 for the LED ring, GPIO17 and GPIO18 for the servos. The other three, 15, 21 and 33, are where the planned host link goes.

VSYS is not a regulated 5 V rail. With USB plugged in it is USB 5 V through a Schottky diode (D1), so about 4.6–4.7 V. On battery it is the cell itself, 3.0–4.2 V, through a P-FET (Q2). Both the LED and servo pages explain when that matters and when to bring your own supply.

items.title: Pins you cannot drive
items.text: The gpio command refuses to drive the pins the board owns — the display, the I2C bus, the touch and IMU interrupts, the UART, and the flash and PSRAM lines. Each has a reason recorded alongside it in main/main.c. gpio set on one of them reports why instead of doing it.

items.title: USB and the serial port
items.text:
USB-C goes only to a CH343P UART bridge on UART0 (GPIO43/44). The ESP32-S3's native USB pins, GPIO19 and GPIO20, are not connected.

Two consequences run through the rest of these pages:

  • The bridge's DTR/RTS lines drive the auto-download circuit, so installing firmware — from the browser, with esptool, or with idf.py flash — needs no buttons.
  • Everything else — the console, uploading clips, updating the firmware — is a serial port, and only one program can hold it at a time. Close idf.py monitor before running any host-side tool.

items.title: Host link: CAN
items.text:
On CAN, the board is a node on a Cyphal bus: Cyphal/CAN, on classic CAN frames. It suits a build that already has a CAN bus through the body and dome, with other Cyphal nodes on it. The board on Cyphal covers what the node does once it's wired: how it gets its node-ID, what it reports, and its settings.

Over Cyphal a controller can do most of what a host does over UART or RS485: move the holo and set its light, apply scenes, show clips and stills, set the LED ring, hear the board's events, list the scenes and the files, and calibrate the holo, as well as manage the node with Cyphal's standard registers and commands (the holo on Cyphal). Uploading files, Wi-Fi and the configuration backup stay on Wi-Fi and the USB console.

items.title: What you need
items.text:
• A CAN transceiver with 3.3 V logic. The ESP32-S3 has the CAN controller, and the transceiver puts it on the wires.

    • A TJA1051T/3 is what this page was written with. It runs from 5 V, and the /3 version has a separate pin (VIO) that sets its logic level to 3.3 V.
    • A 3.3 V part, such as an SN65HVD230 or a TCAN332, needs no 5 V at all.

!!! warning "No 5 V on GPIO33" A 5 V transceiver without a VIO pin (a TJA1050, an MCP2551, or a plain TJA1051T) drives its receive output to 5 V. Use one with VIO, or a 3.3 V part.

  • Twisted pair for CANH and CANL, plus a ground wire.
  • Two 120 Ω resistors, one at each end of the bus.
  • Something to talk to. For a first test, a USB CAN adapter on a computer: one that runs the candleLight (gs_usb) firmware, such as a CANable, works with cyphal_service on Linux and macOS.

items.title: Wiring a TJA1051T/3
items.text:
Transceiver Pin Goes to P2 pin TXD 1 GPIO21 11 GND 2 GND 1 or 5 VCC 3 5 V — RXD 4 GPIO33 12 VIO 5 3V3 6 CANL 6 the bus — CANH 7 the bus — S 8 GND 1 or 5
  • VIO to 3V3. It sets the level of TXD and RXD. Left unconnected, the board receives nothing.
  • S to GND. S high is silent mode: the board hears the bus but never sends, and never acknowledges anyone else's frames; its controller goes bus-off as soon as it tries. Left unconnected, it may float high.
  • 5 V for VCC. The part wants 4.5–5.5 V. P2's VSYS pin is not a 5 V rail: it is about 4.6 V on USB, which is just inside the range, and the cell's voltage on a battery, which is not. Take 5 V from the bus's supply or a regulator.
  • A 100 nF capacitor from VCC to GND, and another from VIO to GND, close to the part.

A 3.3 V transceiver is the same with fewer wires: its supply to 3V3, TXD (often labelled D or CTX) to GPIO21, RXD (R or CRX) to GPIO33, and its mode pin (RS or S) to GND.

GPIO15, the host link's third pin, isn't used on CAN.

items.title: The bus
items.text:
adapter                    board                  another node
  120 Ω H–L                                           120 Ω H–L
  CANH ─────────────────────── CANH ─────────────────────── CANH
  CANL ─────────────────────── CANL ─────────────────────── CANL
   GND ──────────────────────── GND ──────────────────────── GND
  • One line, not a star, with a short stub to each node.
  • 120 Ω across CANH and CANL at each end, and nowhere else. With the power off, a meter across CANH and CANL reads about 60 Ω when both are there, 120 Ω when one is missing, and 40 Ω when there's one too many. Many adapters and modules have a resistor behind a jumper.
  • Even two nodes on a short cable need both resistors. At 1 Mbit/s an unterminated bus doesn't work.
  • Connect the grounds.
  • Every node uses the same bitrate. The board's is 1 Mbit/s unless changed. It samples each bit at 85 % of its length, at every bitrate it offers (20 time quanta; SJW 1): the nearest the ESP32-S3's CAN controller comes to the 87.5 % that CANopen and Cyphal suggest. Nodes a few percent apart work together on a short bus.

items.title: Turning it on
items.text:
On the board's USB console:

link mode can
restart

After the restart the node asks the bus for a node-ID by plug-and-play, and cyphal shows it waiting until an allocator answers:

cyphal: waiting for a node-ID, r2.dome.holo.front, 1 Mbit/s on GPIO21 (TX), GPIO33 (RX)

then running on the node-ID it was given, within a second or two of the start:

cyphal: node 2 (allocated), r2.dome.holo.front, 1 Mbit/s on GPIO21 (TX), GPIO33 (RX)

On a bus with no allocator, give it a fixed node-ID instead, any free one from 0 to 125:

cyphal id 52
cyphal restart

It listens for 2 seconds, then runs:

cyphal: node 52 (fixed), r2.dome.holo.front, 1 Mbit/s on GPIO21 (TX), GPIO33 (RX)

items.title: A first test
items.text:
With a candleLight adapter on a computer, and the board the only other node, give cyphal_service a transport at the board's bitrate. Its allocator is on unless turned off; its database goes to /var/lib/cyphal_service/ unless pnp_db_path says otherwise, which on macOS it has to, since that folder can't be created there without root:

[[transport]]
type        = "can"
name        = "can-usb"
driver      = "gsusb"
node_id     = 43
bitrate     = 1000000
pnp_db_path = "can-usb-allocations.db"

cyphal_service --foreground --config cyphal.toml

Start the board first, so that the service's heartbeats are acknowledged from the moment it opens the adapter. The board asks for a node-ID, the service gives it the lowest one free in its database, and lists it within a second or two:

cyphal> nodes
Transport: can-usb
  Node ID  Uptime(s)  Health     Mode
  2        4          0          0
  43       15         0          0
cyphal> get-info can-usb 2
Node 2  (r2.dome.holo.front)
Hardware : 1.0
Software : 0.0
Unique ID: 68:6f:6c:6f:70:6c:61:79:00:00:e4:b0:63:8c:2d:b0
cyphal> pnp-list
Transport: can-usb
  Node ID  Unique ID (hex)                    Pseudo UID           Timestamp
  2        686f6c6f706c61790000e4b0638c2db0   156728846609014      2026-11-20 09:27:15
  43       7fda830fd867643c1f2cfe147645ebf8   NULL                 2026-04-04 23:43:52

The service records the board's pseudo-ID when it allocates the node-ID, then asks the board for GetInfo and fills in its unique ID. It gives the same node-ID to the same pseudo-ID from then on.

The service also records every node it sees with a fixed node-ID, by its unique ID alone. A board it first saw that way keeps that row, and plug-and-play gives it a new one, with another node-ID: the service matches a plug-and-play request by its pseudo-ID only. To keep the old node-ID, give the board that one as a fixed node-ID, or remove the old row from the service's database.

If the board doesn't appear, cyphal on its console says what the bus looks like from its side:

  • bus-off, and bus-off … times going up while frames: sent doesn't move: the board can't see its own frames on the bus. A CAN controller reads back every bit it sends; when the bus doesn't follow it, each try at a frame ends in an error, and it takes itself off the bus within the first frame. Either the bus doesn't follow TXD (S isn't at GND, so the transceiver is silent, or the TXD wire is loose) or RXD doesn't follow the bus (the RXD wire, or VIO, which sets RXD's level). Check S, VIO, RXD and TXD. The node keeps recovering, less and less often.
  • tx errors at 128 and the state error-passive: the board's frames get onto the bus but nobody acknowledges them. The adapter isn't open, the bitrates differ, CANH and CANL are swapped, or a termination resistor is missing.
  • rx errors climbing: frames arrive damaged. Usually the bitrate, then the termination.
  • frames: sent going up, received 0: something on the bus acknowledges the board's frames but sends nothing: an adapter that is open with no program sending, say. Check that cyphal_service, or the other node, is running.
  • stopped: node-ID … is in use by another node: see a node-ID that is already taken. cyphal_service is node 43 in the configuration above, so a board given 43 stops this way.

The can command tests the wiring below Cyphal: raw frames in and out, and a self-test that needs no second node.

items.title: Host link: I2C
items.text:
Not in the firmware yet

This page describes the I2C link ahead of the firmware, for review. UART and RS485 work now.

On I2C, the board is a target on the host's bus, like a sensor, at an address of its own (0x42 unless changed). It suits a host that already runs an I2C bus through the dome. It speaks native frames through a few registers, and pulls an interrupt line low when it has an event for the host.

This bus is separate from the board's own I2C bus, which serves its touch controller and IMU. Their addresses don't matter here.

items.title: Four wires
items.text: Board P2 pin Host bus GPIO21, SDA 11 SDA GPIO33, SCL 12 SCL GPIO15, IRQ 7 An input, with a pull-up (optional) GND 1 or 5 GND

items.title: Pull-ups
items.text:
An I2C bus needs one pull-up resistor on SDA and one on SCL, to the bus voltage. The board has none on these pins, so the bus must have them somewhere: on the host, on another device, or added.

  • 4.7 kΩ to 3.3 V for 100 kHz on short wires; 2.2 kΩ for longer ones, or 400 kHz.
  • Only one set on the bus, or at least not so many in parallel that the total drops below about 1 kΩ.

items.title: 3.3 V and 5 V
items.text:
The board must never see 5 V on SDA or SCL. On a 5 V bus (an Arduino Uno, most MarcDuinos), put a bidirectional I2C level shifter between the bus and the board: a PCA9306, or a BSS138 module. Its 3.3 V side takes the board and 3.3 V pull-ups, and its 5 V side the host.

Arduino's Wire library pulls the bus up to 5 V

On an AVR, Wire.begin() turns on the chip's own pull-ups, to 5 V. They are weak, but enough to put 5 V on a board wired straight to the bus. Always use a level shifter with a 5 V host.

items.title: Speed and length
items.text:
• 100 kHz is the speed to use. 400 kHz should work on short wires, and will be confirmed when the I2C link is built.
  • I2C is for short runs, a metre or so. Through a slip ring or across a whole droid, use RS485.
  • Clock stretching. The board may hold SCL low briefly at the start of a read. Most hosts wait for it. A Raspberry Pi's I2C hardware doesn't handle stretching reliably: on a Pi, use the i2c-gpio overlay, a software bus that does.

items.title: The interrupt line
items.text:
The board pulls IRQ low while it has events the host hasn't read, and lets it go when there are none. It's open drain: the host needs a pull-up on it, which a microcontroller's internal one usually covers. The IRQ lines of several boards can share one host input.

After an interrupt, the host reads each board's STATUS register, and reads EVENT from each one with pending. A host that doesn't wire IRQ can read STATUS now and then instead.

items.title: Turning it on
items.text:
link mode i2c -a 0x42
restart

Each board on a bus needs its own address, from 0x08 to 0x77, and one no other device on the bus uses.

items.title: Registers
items.text:
Register Access Holds 0x00 STATUS read, 14 bytes The protocol version, what the board is doing, and how many events are waiting 0x10 COMMAND write A command: apply a scene, set the LEDs, move the holo… 0x11 RESULT read The last command's result 0x20 EVENT read, 8 bytes The oldest event not yet read 0x30 VERSION read, 32 bytes The firmware version

The protocol reference has their exact contents.

items.title: A first test, from an Arduino
items.text:
Apply the scene in slot 3, and read the result:

#include <Wire.h>

const uint8_t HOLO = 0x42;

uint16_t crc16(const uint8_t *p, size_t n) {       // CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE
  uint16_t crc = 0xFFFF;
  while (n--) {
    crc ^= (uint16_t)*p++ << 8;
    for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) crc = crc & 0x8000 ? (crc << 1) ^ 0x1021 : crc << 1;
  }
  return crc;
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  Wire.begin();

  uint8_t cmd[] = {0x10, /* seq */ 1, /* SCENE */ 0x10, /* slot */ 3, 0, 0};
  uint16_t crc = crc16(cmd + 1, 3);
  cmd[4] = crc & 0xFF;
  cmd[5] = crc >> 8;
  Wire.beginTransmission(HOLO);
  Wire.write(cmd, sizeof(cmd));
  Wire.endTransmission();

  uint8_t status = 0xFE;
  while (status == 0xFE) {                         // still working
    delay(5);
    Wire.beginTransmission(HOLO);
    Wire.write(0x11);                              // RESULT
    Wire.endTransmission(false);                   // repeated start
    Wire.requestFrom(HOLO, (uint8_t)6);
    Wire.read();                                   // seq
    Wire.read();                                   // type + 0x80
    status = Wire.read();
    Wire.read();                                   // pending
    Wire.read(); Wire.read();                      // crc16
  }
  Serial.println(status == 0 ? "scene 3 applied" : "scene 3 failed");
}

void loop() {}

(The host above is 3.3 V, or behind a level shifter.)

From a Pi, i2cget -y 1 0x42 0x00 reads the first byte of STATUS, the protocol version, which is 1. That's a quick way to check the wiring before writing any code.

items.title: Host link: RS485
items.text:
Not yet tried with a transceiver

RS485 is in the firmware, and its addressing has been tried through a plain UART adapter, but not yet on a bus with a transceiver.

RS485 is the host link for long runs and for several boards on one bus. It is the UART over a twisted pair, through a small transceiver on each board: runs of tens of metres work, it shrugs off the noise of motors, and it passes through a slip ring. It carries both JSON lines and native frames, with an address on every request.

RS485 here is half duplex: one pair of wires, used by one device at a time. The host is in charge. It sends a request to one board, and only that board answers. Boards never speak unasked, so events are fetched rather than pushed.

items.title: What you need
items.text:
• A 3.3 V RS485 transceiver for each board: a MAX3485, SP3485 or THVD1410, or a module built on one.

!!! warning "Not the common blue MAX485 module" The MAX485 is a 5 V part, and its receive output would put 5 V on GPIO33. Use a 3.3 V part, or a module that says it's 3.3 V.

  • A transceiver for the host. A USB-RS485 adapter for a computer or Pi (one with automatic direction control, such as FTDI's USB-RS485-WE), an RS485 HAT, or another transceiver for a microcontroller.
  • Twisted pair for A and B, such as one pair of a Cat5 cable, plus a ground wire.
  • Two 120 Ω resistors, one at each end of the bus.

items.title: Wiring a board
items.text:
Transceiver Board P2 pin DI (driver in) GPIO21 11 RO (receiver out) GPIO33 12 DE and /RE, joined GPIO15 7 VCC 3V3 6 GND GND 1 or 5

The board drives GPIO15 high while it sends, and low the rest of the time, so it listens unless it's answering.

A module with automatic direction control (no DE or /RE pins) works too: leave GPIO15 unconnected.

items.title: The bus
items.text:
host                     board 1                  board 2
  120 Ω A–B                                           120 Ω A–B
     A ──────────────────────── A ──────────────────────── A
     B ──────────────────────── B ──────────────────────── B
   GND ────────────────────── GND ────────────────────── GND
  • One line, not a star. Run the pair from board to board, with only a short stub to each.
  • 120 Ω across A and B at each end, and nowhere else. Many transceiver modules have one fitted: remove it, or leave its jumper open, on every board but the last.
  • Bias, once, at the host. A pull-up from A to 3.3 V and a pull-down from B to GND (680 Ω each) keep the idle bus in a known state. USB adapters and HATs often have these already.
  • Connect the grounds. RS485 tolerates some difference between them, but not an unlimited one, and the boards may be on separate supplies.
  • A and B aren't always labelled the same way. If nothing is heard, swap them at one end.

A standard transceiver is one "unit load", and a bus takes 32. Parts rated at 1/8 of a unit load (the THVD1410 is one) allow 256.

items.title: Turning it on
items.text:
Give each board its own address, from 1 to 223, on its USB console:

link mode rs485 -b 115200 -a 3
restart

Groups let one request reach several boards: a board in groups 2 and 5 answers requests to its own address, and acts on requests to @g2 and @g5, without answering them.

link groups 2 5

Every board on a bus must use the same baud rate.

items.title: Talking to a board
items.text:
Every request names a board with @, and the reply carries its address:

> @3 POST /scenes/apply {"name":"cantina"}
< @3 200 {"screen":{...},"leds":{...},"holo":{...}}
> @g2 POST /scenes/end
                                       (no reply: a group request isn't answered)
> @* PATCH /leds {"mode":"off"}
                                       (no reply)

A line without @ is ignored on RS485, and counted in link.

  • Wait for each reply, or 2 seconds, before the next request.
  • After a request to a group or to every board, leave 10 ms before the next request, so every board has read it.
  • The board waits 1 ms before it answers, for the host's transceiver to stop sending. A host that turns around more slowly can ask for longer: reply_delay_ms, 0–50, in the link settings.

items.title: Events on a bus
items.text:
Nobody on the bus speaks unasked, so the host polls for what happened (clip_ended, scene_ended, touch); a resource's changes are only pushed, on UART, so here the host reads the resource when it wants it. It doesn't need to poll hard, because every reply says how many events are waiting on the board that sent it:

> @3 GET /screen
< @3 200 +1 {"powered":true,"showing":"nothing",...}
> @3 GET /link/events
< @3 200 {"seq":7,"lost":0,"events":[{"event":"scene_ended","seq":7,"name":"cantina",...}]}

A host that isn't otherwise talking to a board sends it a cheap request now and then, such as GET /link, or the native STATUS, and fetches events when the count isn't 0.

Ask each board for the events it should report first, with @3 PATCH /link/events {"kinds":["scene_ended"]}, or once and for all in its saved settings with link events scene_ended.

items.title: A first test
items.text:
With a USB-RS485 adapter on a computer, and one board on the bus, open the adapter in a terminal at the board's baud rate and send:

@3 GET /link

If nothing comes back, run link log on on the board's USB console and try again:

  • Nothing arrives: check A and B (swap them), the ground, and that the adapter's direction control is automatic.
  • Lines arrive, but no reply: the address in the line isn't the board's.
  • The reply is garbled at the host: try a longer reply_delay_ms.

items.title: Host link: UART
items.text:
A UART is the simplest host link: three wires to one host close by, such as a Raspberry Pi, an ESP32, an Arduino with a spare serial port, or a USB-serial adapter on a computer. It carries both JSON lines and native frames, and the board can send events as they happen without an extra wire.

The board's UART is 8 data bits, no parity, one stop bit (8N1), at 115200 baud unless changed, with no flow control.

items.title: Three wires
items.text:
The board's TX goes to the host's RX, and the host's TX to the board's RX.

Board P2 pin Host GPIO21, TX 11 RX GPIO33, RX 12 TX, through a divider if the host is 5 V (below) GND 1 or 5 GND. Always connect it GPIO15, ATTN (optional) 7 An input that can wake the host

Keep the wires under a metre or two. For longer runs, or anything through a slip ring, use RS485.

items.title: 3.3 V and 5 V
items.text:
The board's pins are 3.3 V, and 5 V on GPIO33 will damage it.

  • A 3.3 V host (a Pi, an ESP32, a 3.3 V Arduino, a 3.3 V USB-serial adapter): wire it directly.
  • A 5 V host (an Arduino Uno, Mega or Nano, most MarcDuinos): its TX needs bringing down to 3.3 V. A divider is enough at 115200 baud: 1 kΩ from the host's TX to GPIO33, and 2 kΩ from GPIO33 to GND. The other direction needs nothing: a 5 V AVR reads the board's 3.3 V as a high. A level-shifter module (BSS138 or TXS0108 style) works in both directions instead.

Check a USB-serial adapter's voltage before connecting it. Many have a 5 V / 3.3 V jumper, and some are 5 V only.

items.title: ATTN, for a host that sleeps
items.text: The board sends events on its TX line as they happen, so most hosts don't need a third wire. A host that sleeps can't be woken by a UART line alone. For that, turn on attn in the link settings and wire GPIO15 to an input that wakes it. ATTN goes low while events are waiting, and high again once the host has read them.

items.title: Turning it on
items.text:
On the board's USB console:

link mode uart -b 115200
restart

items.title: A first test, from a computer
items.text:
With a 3.3 V USB-serial adapter on the three wires, open it in any terminal program at 115200 baud, 8N1. After the board restarts, it sends:

! {"event":"ready","firmware":"v1.1.0","protocol":1,"address":1}

Type a request and press Enter. The board doesn't echo it, so turn on local echo in the terminal to see what you type:

GET /leds
200 {"mode":"off","colour":"#ffffff","loop":false,"brightness":30,"count":16,"gpio":16}
PATCH /leds {"mode":"solid","colour":"orange"}
200 {"mode":"solid","colour":"#ffa500","loop":false,"brightness":30,"count":16,"gpio":16}

Or use tools/hostlink.py from the repository, which sends a request and prints the reply, sends native frames, and follows events (it needs pip install pyserial):

tools/hostlink.py /dev/cu.usbserial-X GET /leds
tools/hostlink.py /dev/cu.usbserial-X --native status
tools/hostlink.py /dev/cu.usbserial-X --listen scene_ended,leds

If nothing comes back, run link log on on the USB console and try again. Nothing arriving means the wiring (TX and RX swapped is the usual fault). Garbage, or framing_errors climbing in link, means the baud rates differ.

items.title: From a Raspberry Pi
items.text:
The Pi's own UART is on its 40-pin header: TX on pin 8 (GPIO14), RX on pin 10 (GPIO15), and GND on pin 6. Both are 3.3 V, so wire them straight to the board. Turn the serial port on and its login shell off with sudo raspi-config (Interface Options, Serial Port), then use /dev/serial0.

In Python, with pyserial:

import json
import serial

port = serial.Serial("/dev/serial0", 115200, timeout=2)

def request(line):
    """Send one request, and return (status, body). Events that arrive first are printed."""
    port.write((line + "\n").encode())
    while True:
        reply = port.readline().decode().strip()
        if not reply:
            raise TimeoutError(line)
        if reply.startswith("!"):
            print("event:", json.loads(reply[2:]))
            continue
        status, _, rest = reply.partition(" ")
        if rest.startswith("+"):                   # events waiting: +<n>
            _, _, rest = rest.partition(" ")
        return int(status), json.loads(rest) if rest else None

request('PATCH /link/events {"kinds":["scene_ended"],"push":true}')
print(request('POST /scenes/apply {"name":"cantina"}'))

items.title: From an ESP32
items.text:
Any of its spare UARTs, on any two pins, wired straight across. With the Arduino core:

HardwareSerial holo(1);

void setup() {
  holo.begin(115200, SERIAL_8N1, /* rx */ 16, /* tx */ 17);
  holo.println("POST /scenes/apply {\"name\":\"cantina\"}");
}

void loop() {
  if (holo.available()) {
    String line = holo.readStringUntil('\n');
    if (line.startsWith("!")) {
      // an event: parse line.substring(2) with ArduinoJson
    } else {
      // a reply: the status is the first three characters
    }
  }
}

items.title: From a 5 V Arduino
items.text:
Through the divider above. An Uno has one hardware serial port, and it's also its USB, so use a Mega's Serial1, or SoftwareSerial at 9600 or 19200 baud (link mode uart -b 19200). SoftwareSerial can't send and receive at once, so leave events unpushed and use the pending count instead.

With little memory, native frames are easier than JSON. A SCENE request for slot 3 is these bytes before COBS: the board's address (1), a sequence number the reply carries back (7), the type (0x10), the slot, and the CRC:

01 07 10 03 <crc16, low byte first>

JSON lines work too, as long as the host only writes them and reads the status:

Serial1.begin(115200);
Serial1.println("POST /scenes/apply {\"name\":\"cantina\"}");
// the reply starts with "200" when it worked

items.title: Wiring the LED ring
items.text:
The firmware drives a 16-LED WS2812 ring on GPIO16, using Espressif's led_strip component on the RMT peripheral, in GRB order at 800 kHz. The strip is cleared at boot.

For what to do with it once it is wired, see LED patterns.

items.title: Three wires
items.text:
GPIO16 is pin 8 of the P2 header.

Strip P2 pin Signal DIN (data in — the tail of the arrow printed on the strip) 8 GPIO16, through a 300–500 Ω resistor at the strip end GND 1 or 5 Ground. Always connect it, even when the strip has its own supply +5 V 2 VSYS, or a separate 5 V supply — see below

The series resistor goes at the strip, not at the board: it is there to damp reflections on the data line, and it only does that near the far end.

items.title: Power
items.text:
Each WS2812 draws up to about 60 mA at full white, so sixteen of them can ask for 1 A. That is too much for a single SH1.0 contact and its thin wire, and too much for a USB port that is also powering the board.

  • From VSYS (P2 pin 2). Keep leds bright at 30 or below, which is roughly 300 mA. Note that VSYS is about 4.6–4.7 V on USB and 3.0–4.2 V on battery, not a clean 5 V.
  • From a separate supply. For full brightness, feed the strip's +5 V from the supply directly and join the grounds. The board and the strip must share a ground reference or the data signal has nothing to be measured against.
  • Always put a 470–1000 µF capacitor across the strip's +5 V and GND, at the strip, to absorb the current steps as LEDs switch.
  • A 12 V WS2811 strip needs its own 12 V supply. Share only GND and DIN with the board; 12 V on P2 would destroy it.

items.title: Data level
items.text:
GPIO16 drives 3.3 V. A WS281x wants 0.7 × its own supply voltage as a logic high — 3.3 V when the strip runs from VSYS on USB, and 3.5 V from a true 5 V supply. So the margin is nil to negative, though short wires usually work anyway.

If the first LED flickers or shows the wrong colour while the rest behave, that is the symptom. Add a 74AHCT1G125 buffer between GPIO16 and DIN, powered from the strip's +5 V: an HCT input treats 3.3 V as a solid high and re-drives it at 5 V.

items.title: Data rate
items.text:
800 kHz is correct for WS2812, WS2812B and SK6812, and is the default.

If the LEDs stay white whatever you send, the rate is wrong

menuconfig also offers 400 kHz, for WS2811 strips. At 400 kHz a "0" bit is sent as a 0.5 µs pulse, and a WS2812 reads that as a "1". Every frame then comes out as full white — including the frame that is supposed to turn the LEDs off, which is what makes it confusing rather than merely wrong.

items.title: A note on GPIO16
items.text: GPIO16 is the ESP32-S3's XTAL_32K_N pin. This board has no 32 kHz crystal fitted, so it is an ordinary GPIO and free to use. The gpio command still refuses to drive it, because the firmware has claimed it for the strip.

items.title: Mounting the screen in the dome
items.text: A holoprojector's lens sits over the panel, and both how the panel is centred under it and which way round it is rotated show up in every clip afterwards. screen calibration puts up a pattern made for judging exactly those two things by eye, while the board is in your hand and before anything is glued or tightened.

items.title: The pattern
items.text:
screen calibration

A white crosshair on black: one line across the panel's full width, one down its full height, and a solid arrowhead sitting on the vertical line just above the crossing, pointing up.

What `screen calibration` puts on the panel, pixel for pixel.

Both lines are two pixels thick. The panel is 240 pixels across, so its centre falls on the seam between pixels 119 and 120 rather than on a pixel, and each line straddles that seam — the crossing is the panel's true centre, not a pixel either side of it. If a line looks off-centre behind the lens, it is the mounting, not the firmware.

The pattern stays up until something else is shown. screen on its own reports it, and screen clear takes it down and puts the panel back to sleep.

The picture above is generated from the firmware's own geometry by tools/render_calibration.py, and make docs-check fails if the two ever disagree.

screen calib does the same thing

Alignment is fiddly and the command gets typed a lot. Both spellings work.

items.title: Aligning
items.text:
1. Flash the firmware and open the console — see Install.
  2. Run screen calibration. The panel wakes with the pattern already in place.
  3. Hold or rest the board in the dome and centre it: the crossing goes in the middle of the lens opening, and the two lines should reach the edge of the aperture by the same amount all the way round.
  4. Rotate it until the arrow points at the top of the dome. This is the only part of the pattern that is not symmetric, and it is the whole reason it is there — a crosshair alone looks right at all four rotations.
  5. Fix the panel in place, then run screen calibration again and check nothing shifted while you were tightening it.
  6. screen clear when you are done.

If the dome's aperture is smaller than the panel, aim for the lines being cut off equally on opposite sides rather than for seeing all four arms in full.

items.title: Judging brightness at the same time
items.text:
The lit area's edge is much easier to see at a low backlight, and a dim panel is also the honest test of whether the lens is sitting flat:

lcd bl 20
screen calibration

lcd bl 100 puts it back. The level survives until the next restart; see Console commands.

items.title: Why this carries over to clips
items.text:
video play draws every frame centred on the same 240×240 panel, so the crossing is where a clip's centre lands and the arrow is which way a clip's "up" points. Align the crosshair and the clips are aligned; there is no separate offset or rotation setting in the firmware to correct for a panel that went in crooked.

A clip is the final check. Put one on the board and play it — see Video clips — and the pattern has done its job if the picture is centred in the lens and the right way up.

The panel is round, the frame is square

The GC9A01 is a 240×240 panel with a circular visible area, so the very ends of the crosshair's arms disappear under the bezel. That is the panel, not a drawing error — the lines do run the full width and height.

items.title: Wiring the servos
items.text:
Two hobby servos aim the holoprojector: pan (left and right) and tilt (up and down). They run on the ESP32-S3's MCPWM, one timer each.

For the motions themselves, and for calibrating each axis, see The holoprojector.

items.title: Connections
items.text:
GPIO17 and GPIO18 are pins 9 and 10 of the P2 header.

Wire Goes to Servo 1 signal (orange, or white) P2 pin 9, GPIO17 Servo 2 signal P2 pin 10, GPIO18 Both servos' power (red) A separate 5 V supply Both servos' ground (brown, or black) That supply's ground, and P2 pin 1 or 5

items.title: Power
items.text:
Do not take servo power from P2's VSYS pin

A small hobby servo draws 0.5–1 A as it starts moving or when it stalls. Two of them at once would brown out the board, and a brown-out mid-write is how filesystems get damaged. Give the servos their own 5 V supply.

Join the servo supply's ground to the board's ground. The pulse the board sends is measured against ground, so without a shared reference the servos see noise rather than a signal.

items.title: Signal level
items.text: The signal is 3.3 V, which hobby servos accept — unlike the LED strip, a servo's input is a comparator with a low threshold, so no level shifting is needed.

items.title: Which servo is which
items.text:
By default servo 1 (GPIO17) pans and servo 2 (GPIO18) tilts.

The sketch this firmware grew out of never recorded which servo was which, so if holo wag nods instead of shaking its head, the two are swapped. Rather than rewiring, change Which servo pans in idf.py menuconfig — see Configuration.

items.title: Travel
items.text:
Each servo has a working range, defaulting to the range the original sketch used: 1150–1900 µs for servo 1 and 1300–1950 µs for servo 2. Both sit inside an absolute 1000–2000 µs range that no servo is ever driven outside, whatever it is asked for.
