State Means off The host link isn't running in CAN mode: link mode can, then restart waiting for a node-ID Asking the bus for one by plug-and-play, and no allocator has answered yet; or one has, and the node is still in the second it listens before taking it up listening, before going online as node 52 (fixed) The 2 seconds before a node with a fixed node-ID starts node 52 (allocated) or (fixed) Running stopped: node-ID 52 is in use by another node Stopped, until told to start again not started on GPIO21 and GPIO33: … The CAN controller didn't start at the board's start (out of memory, say): the host link then holds no pins (link says can didn't start), and only a restart of the board tries again. Or a cyphal restart failed: the controller didn't start again, or would not stop, in which case the node is stopped and the controller still runs. cyphal restart tries again

The bus's state is CAN's own, read from the two error counters beside it (the larger of them):

State Means error-active Normal: both counters under 96 error-warning A counter at 96 or more: errors lately, not yet enough to change how the controller behaves error-passive A counter at 128 or more: many errors lately. A board alone on the bus sits here, with tx errors 128, since nobody acknowledges its frames bus-off So many transmit errors that the controller has taken itself off the bus. The node brings it back by itself, and counts how often

items.title: Bus-off
items.text:
A controller goes bus-off when its frames keep failing in a way that is its own fault: it sends a bit and doesn't see that bit on the bus. On a working bus that is rare, and the node brings the controller back within a second, with a warning in the board's log:

W (4663) cyphal: bus-off (1 times since the start): recovering

When the board can't see its own bits at all (the transceiver's S pin high, or its VIO, RXD or TXD not connected: what to check), every frame it sends takes it bus-off again within a moment of each recovery. So when a bus-off comes less than a minute after the recovery before it, the node waits before recovering: 1 s, then 2, 4, 8 and 16 s, and 30 s from then on, until the bus has stayed up for a minute. The log says so at the 2nd bus-off in a row, the 4th, the 8th, and so on, ever further apart:

W (5663) cyphal: bus-off again, 2 times in a row (2 since the start): recovering in 1 s; logged again at 4 in a row
W (10693) cyphal: bus-off again, 4 times in a row (4 since the start): recovering in 4 s; logged again at 8 in a row
W (72883) cyphal: bus-off again, 8 times in a row (8 since the start): recovering in 30 s; logged again at 16 in a row

and cyphal shows the wait:

  bus: bus-off, tx errors 128, rx errors 0, bus-off 7 times (back to back: recovering in 21 s)
  transfers: sent 7, received 0; frames: sent 0, received 0; dropped 41
  up 50 s; frames given to the controller 7, not sent 6, waiting 1; not read (queue full) 0

Each bus-off costs the frame that was on the wire (not sent); the heartbeats due meanwhile expire (dropped, about one a second). The rest of the board runs as usual.

items.title: The holo on Cyphal
items.text:
A controller on the bus, the dome panel or an app on a Linux machine, can do with this holo what the panel does with a holo of its own: every motion, the light, direct moves of the axes, the holo's state, and letting go of the servos. It also reaches most of the board's own features: scenes, the screen, the LED ring, the board's events, and the lists of scenes and files. And the node is managed the standard Cyphal way, with registers and commands, by any Cyphal tool, the holo's calibration among them. The Cyphal interface reference has every type, port and register.

The holo's messages and services are Cyphal data types of their own, r2.holo.*, kept in the r2_cyphal_dsdl repository, which a controller generates its code from. Everything else (the heartbeat, GetInfo, registers, restart) uses Cyphal's standard types.

items.title: What a controller can do
items.text:
To It Default port Know what the holo is doing Subscribes to r2.holo.Status subject 2300 Hear what happens: clips and scenes starting and ending, touches Subscribes to r2.holo.Event subject 2301 Know where the axes are Subscribes to r2.holo.Axes subject 2302 Move the axes directly Publishes r2.holo.Axes, a stream of setpoints subject 2303 Start a motion Calls r2.holo.Motion service 100 Set the holo's light Calls r2.holo.Light service 101 Apply or end a scene Calls r2.holo.Scene service 102 Show a clip, an image or a colour, or nothing; set the backlight Calls r2.holo.Screen service 103 Set the LED ring Calls r2.holo.Ring service 104 List the saved scenes Calls r2.holo.ListScenes service 105 Ask what a clip or an image is Calls r2.holo.MediaInfo service 106 List the files, and their sizes Calls uavcan.file.List and uavcan.file.GetInfo services 406, 405 Change a setting, a port's number, the holo's calibration Calls uavcan.register.Access service 384 Restart the board, reset it, find it Calls uavcan.node.ExecuteCommand service 435

Each service does what the same request over the HTTP API or the host link does, through the same code, and refuses it for the same reasons: the answer carries the host link's status code (ok, bad request, not found, not playable, not ready, busy, failed) and the message in words, such as holo: refused, uncalibrated (tilt).

items.title: Moving the holo
items.text:
r2.holo.Motion starts any of the holo's motions, with every parameter the console's holo takes: center, move, nudge, twitch, wag, nod, scan, circle, stop, and off, which stops, lets both servos go limp and turns the light (the ring) off. A parameter left at 0 takes the motion's default, as on the console. It runs the HTTP API's own POST /holo/motion, so a motion out of range is refused in the same words. A twitch or a scan takes a time limit, but a scan does not stop by it today, here or on the console or the HTTP API: a fault in the holo engine the board shares with the dome panel. Stop a scan with stop (or another motion) instead.

For a direct move, a controller streams setpoints instead: r2.holo.Axes messages with both axes in hundredths of a percent of their travel each side of the centre (−10000 to 10000). Each setpoint goes to the servos at once, with no easing, and stops any motion running first; the latest wins. This is what a joystick or a ROS joint command needs. The holo publishes where it has put the axes on the same scale, ten times a second while it moves and once a second at rest. On the bench, a 50-a-second stream reached the board whole, each setpoint at the servos at once, and stopped a twitch that was running.

A subject belongs to the whole bus, so two holos listening for setpoints on the same subject move together. Give a second holo its own setpoint subject by its register, uavcan.sub.setpoint.id.

items.title: The light is the LED ring
items.text:
A dome panel's own holos have a single-colour light: off, on, pulse, flicker and blink, at a level, each for good or for a time, after which the light goes back to what it was doing; and leia, the message from Leia, a flicker at full with the holo turned to the centre. On this board r2.holo.Light does all of that on the LED ring: on lights it steady, and the others are ring modes of the same names. The ring keeps its colour unless the request gives one.

The level is a share of the ring's brightness, not a brightness of its own: the light at 100 is the ring at the brightness it is set to (leds bright, or the board's settings), so a controller can't light a ring powered from the board past its limit. The ring has pulse and blink, and timed modes, for this; the console's leds and the HTTP API have them too. The console's holo led and holo leia belong to the holo engine shared with the panel, and still do nothing on this board.

items.title: Knowing what it is doing
items.text:
r2.holo.Status is one message with everything: the holo's motion (ready or why not, what runs, for how long, why the last one stopped early, the last motion asked for), the ring (including a timed mode and what it goes back to), the screen (what shows, a clip's progress, the backlight) and the scene running to its end. It goes out within a quarter of a second of a change, and once a second whatever changes.

r2.holo.Event carries the board's happenings, the same ones as its JSON events: a clip or a scene starting or ending, with its path or name, and a touch on the screen while touch reporting is on. Each is numbered with the board's sequence number, the one the web app and the host link see. There is no catching up on Cyphal: a controller that sees a number skipped has missed something, and reads the next Status for how things are now.

items.title: Scenes, the screen and the ring
items.text: r2.holo.Scene applies a saved scene by its slot or its name, or ends the one running to its end; r2.holo.Screen shows a clip, an image, a colour, the crosshair or nothing, and sets the backlight; r2.holo.Ring sets the LED ring's mode, colour, loop, period and brightness. Each runs the HTTP API's own code, so a missing file is refused as not found and one the screen can't show as not playable, in the same words. Showing a still decodes it, which takes up to a few hundred milliseconds: Scene and Screen requests are carried out one at a time by a task of their own, so the holo's setpoints and the board's Status never wait for them, and a controller waits for each response before it counts on the next request being done after it. The scenes themselves are made in the web app or with the HTTP API.

items.title: The lists
items.text: r2.holo.ListScenes gives the saved scenes one a call, by index, with their slots, in the order GET /api/v1/scenes has them. The standard uavcan.file.List and uavcan.file.GetInfo give the files on the board, as fs ls sees them: a directory's entries one a call, by index, in order of their names (a directory's with / after it), and each one's size and when it was last written. r2.holo.MediaInfo gives a clip's or an image's details from its header (its kind, size, frames, rate and length) and whether the screen can show it, and why not, as GET /api/v1/media/info does. All of them only read: files and scenes are made and changed over Wi-Fi. While the board is busy with earlier requests, uavcan.file.List isn't answered at all (its empty name would end the list), so a client asks again after its timeout. The reference has the details and the times on the bench.

items.title: Settings as registers
items.text:
The node's settings are Cyphal registers, which any Cyphal tool lists, reads and writes:

Register The setting Default uavcan.node.id The node-ID, 0–127; 65535 for plug-and-play (cyphal id) 65535 r2.node.name The name GetInfo reports (cyphal name) r2.dome.holo.front uavcan.can.bitrate The bitrate (cyphal bitrate) 1000000 uavcan.pub.status.id, … uavcan.srv.ring.id, … Each port's number; 65535 turns the port off The defaults above r2.holo.horizontal.endpoints_us, r2.holo.vertical.endpoints_us Each axis's closed and open ends in µs (holo endpoints); 0 0 clears them The default range, not saved r2.holo.horizontal.release, …vertical.release, …settle_ms Each servo's drive policy (the web app's, PUT /api/v1/servos/policy) Hold everywhere, 100 ms r2.touch.reporting Touch events on or off, saved: the board's touch setting (settings touch; touch on and touch off don't save) Off

They are the same saved settings the cyphal commands change, and the console reads and writes the registers by name too:

cyphal register
cyphal register uavcan.sub.setpoint.id
cyphal register uavcan.sub.setpoint.id 2313

uavcan.sub.setpoint.id          2313                   natural16[1], mutable, persistent; 2303 until the node's next start

A change takes effect when the node next starts (cyphal restart). A value the board can't take is refused with the reason, and the register keeps its value:

cyphal: uavcan.sub.setpoint.id not written: a subject-ID is 0 to 8191, or 65535 to turn the port off

A number another port already has is refused as well, with the port that has it: the subjects, published or subscribed, are one set and the services another, and the node's own standard ports count (the rule). To swap two ports' numbers, move one to a free number, or to 65535, first.

Over Cyphal the response says the same by carrying the old value.

The holo's calibration registers take effect at once, and are the servos' own saved values, the ones holo endpoints, the web app's calibration and PUT /api/v1/servos/policy change: a change either way shows the other way, at once. Writing 0 0 to an axis's endpoints clears its drive policy too, as holo endpoints <axis> clear does. Touch reporting is one of the board's settings (settings touch, touch.reporting in /api/v1/settings): saved, applied at once and at every start; touch on and touch off change it until the next start, and the register reads what is in effect.

The port numbers are saved and go into a backup with the rest of the node's settings. A second holo restored from the same backup needs its own node-ID and its own setpoint subject.

items.title: Restart, factory reset, identify
items.text:
uavcan.node.ExecuteCommand, the standard command service:

  • restart restarts the board, a second after it answers;
  • factory reset puts the node's registers and the board's settings (touch reporting among them) back to their defaults and restarts, keeping the scenes, the files, the servos' calibration and drive policy, the network settings and the host link's mode (so the node comes back on the bus, asking for a node-ID by plug-and-play);
  • identify blinks the ring white and shows the crosshair for 5 seconds, to tell which board on the bus is which, then puts both back. It runs as a short scene called identify, so the web app shows it, and it ends a scene that was running.

Every other command, power off and emergency stop among them, is refused as a bad command. The board's log says which node asked.

items.title: From a computer
items.text:
Yakut speaks all of this, given the standard types and r2_cyphal_dsdl on its CYPHAL_PATH: the folders that hold uavcan and r2. With the board at node-ID 52, it would read a register, start a wag, and restart the board:

export CYPHAL_PATH="$HOME/public_regulated_data_types:$HOME/r2_cyphal_dsdl"
yakut register-access 52 uavcan.srv.motion.id
yakut call 52 motion '{motion: {kind: 4, count: 3}}'
yakut execute-command 52 restart

On macOS a gs_usb adapter (a CANable, candleLight) needs a workaround first: python-can, which Yakut uses, asks the system to detach a kernel driver, and macOS refuses without root. This repository's tools/yakut_can.py runs Yakut with it, and with the adapter opened and closed only while the board is quiet, which a candleLight needs; it sets the transport and CYPHAL_PATH from the repository's own copies of the types, and wants the board on a fixed node-ID:

tools/yakut_can.py register-list 52
tools/yakut_can.py register-access 52 uavcan.srv.motion.id
tools/yakut_can.py register-access 52 uavcan.pub.status.id 2310

It refuses execute-command (which newer versions of the click library name execute), and a call to uavcan.node.ExecuteCommand: on the bench, with the adapter's earlier firmware (a canable.io build of candleLight, until 2026-11-21), the candleLight now and then stopped passing frames to the computer during a Yakut session, every time a command was sent and sometimes otherwise, and only the adapter's own bootloader brought it back. Its firmware has since been replaced by a build of candleLight's current main branch, on which Yakut hasn't been tried; the refusal stays until it has. The repository's hardware tests send the commands instead. It also refuses what would leave the board never quiet when the adapter has to close (a write of 65535, plug-and-play, to uavcan.node.id: use cyphal id auto on the console), register-batch, and a --bitrate other than the board's.

items.title: What stays off Cyphal
items.text:
Uploading clips and images, the network and the web app's settings, passwords, the configuration backup and firmware updates stay on Wi-Fi and the USB console. So do saving and editing scenes: Cyphal applies a saved one. The reference has the whole list.

transfers counts what was sent, whole (heartbeats, port lists, responses and plug-and-play requests) and what was received (requests and plug-and-play messages); frames counts what the controller sent and had acknowledged, and what it received. dropped counts transfers the board gave up on because the bus didn't take them in time (a second, a heartbeat's period), or that it couldn't queue or put together at all. It rises while the board is alone on the bus, about once a second as each heartbeat expires (a little less while it waits for a node-ID: each request expires in turn, and the next isn't queued until it has), and shouldn't otherwise. The frame the controller was retrying then goes out when another node turns up, a little late.

The next two lines are for when something seems wrong: how long the node has run, frames it handed to the controller that were never sent (bus-off, or a restart of the node), frames that arrived faster than they could be read, the most frames its transmit queue has held since the start (of the 160 it can), and the memory it uses. Its libcanard heap is 32 KB of PSRAM, reserved at its first start; a port list waiting to go takes about 1.8 KB of it. The internal RAM it takes is its task's 3 KB stack while it runs, the worker's 4.5 KB stack (the task that writes registers and reads the holo's, carries out the holo's Motion, Light, Ring and ListScenes requests and its setpoints, and builds what the holo publishes, so that the node's own never waits) from its first start on, the second worker's 7.5 KB stack (the task that carries out Scene, Screen and MediaInfo requests, the file services and identify, which may decode an image, read a file whole or wait for the storage volume; the host link's own task, which runs the same routes on 10 KB, doesn't run while the node has its pins), and the CAN driver's queues (about 8 KB, kept once the controller has run, the same as for can). The holo's mailboxes and the worker's copy of Status are in PSRAM.

services counts the register and command requests, the ones refused, and those answered busy because the worker already held four, or the second worker two, or left unanswered for that reason (a read of one of the holo's servo registers, a uavcan.file.List: their types can't say busy, and the client asks again); worker shows how many each holds now. application counts the holo's own: requests to its services handed to the workers and setpoints received, and gives the health the heartbeat reports. published counts each message the holo publishes, Status, Event and Axes, that was queued for the bus, and in brackets, for Status and Axes, those a newer one replaced before they went (none, on a quiet bus), and for Event, those its full queue refused (each offer refused: the Event is offered again a moment later, and the happenings after it are read from the board's record once it has gone). A message waits in its mailbox until the transmit queue has room for the whole of it; one queued that then waited there past its second is counted with the transfers dropped.

items.title: Testing the wiring: raw frames
items.text:
The can command works below Cyphal: plain CAN frames, for checking a transceiver and a bus. It uses the same pins and the same controller, so it runs only while the Cyphal node is off (link mode off), and the node won't start while it's running. While the node holds the controller, can alone still reports the bus (its first line ends for the Cyphal node), and every can sub-command refuses:

can: the controller is in use by the Cyphal node: `can` only reports while it is
Command Does can Whether it's running, the bus's state and error counters, and frames sent and received can start [-b <bitrate>] [--listen\|--selftest] Start the controller, at 1 Mbit/s unless told otherwise. --listen receives without sending or acknowledging. --selftest receives its own frames and needs no acknowledgement can stop Stop, and release the pins as floating inputs. dump and echo go off, so the next can start is quiet can send <id>#<hex> Send one frame. An ID of up to three hex digits is an 11-bit one; eight digits, a 29-bit one. Up to 8 data bytes can dump [on\|off] Print every frame received, until turned off (on if neither is given) can echo [on\|off] Send every frame received straight back, with 1 added to its ID can recover Bring the controller back from bus-off

With no second node, a self-test shows that the controller, the two pins and the transceiver work:

can start --selftest
can dump on
can send 123#DEADBEEF

The frame comes back:

can: 123 [4] DE AD BE EF

can stop ends the self-test. A board that can't see its own bits on the bus fails it: the frame never comes back, and the controller goes bus-off at once (can reads bus-off, bus-off 1 times, waiting to send 1). The transceiver's S pin high (silent), or its VIO, RXD or TXD not connected, does that.

With an adapter on the bus, can start and can dump on show what it sends, and can send 1ABCDEF0#0102 should arrive there. A frame that is sent but never acknowledged leaves tx errors climbing: a first test lists what to check.

can alone reports:

can: running at 1 Mbit/s on GPIO21 (TX), GPIO33 (RX), normal
  bus: error-active, tx errors 0, rx errors 0, bus errors 0, bus-off 0 times
  frames: sent 4, received 1000; send failed 0, receive dropped 0 (queue held 5 of 256 at most), waiting to send 0
  dump off, echo off; internal heap 107259 bytes free, 69388 lowest

bus errors counts every error the controller has seen on the bus since can start, not counting lost arbitration: thousands a second while nobody acknowledges, since each retry of the frame is one. send failed counts frames that never made it: the one on the wire when the controller went bus-off, and any still waiting at can stop. While the controller is bus-off, can send refuses (can: bus-off: `can recover` first); frames already waiting behind the bus-off go out after can recover, which brings the controller back once the bus has been idle for 128 periods of 11 bits. Unlike the node, can never recovers by itself. receive dropped counts frames that arrived faster than the board could take them, which can dump causes on a busy bus: printing is slower than CAN. The queue between the controller and the board's reader holds 256 frames, enough to ride out a flash write on a bus full of 8-byte frames; queue held says how full it has been since can start. With --listen, the bus always reads error-passive with rx errors 128: that keeps the controller from ever sending an error flag. While can runs, gpio refuses its two pins.

tools/can_check.py, in this repository, is the computer's side, through a gs_usb adapter (candleLight, CANable): listen, send, flood, and echo, which sends numbered frames to a board running can echo on and checks that every one comes back, in order. An adapter keeps retrying a frame nobody acknowledged, even after it is closed and opened again; can start on the board acknowledges it and clears it.

items.title: Files on the board
items.text: Clips live on an 11 MB LittleFS volume mounted at /data. It is formatted empty on first boot, and filled over the serial console — there is no SD card and no USB mass storage.

items.title: On the board
items.text:
The fs command works on the volume; every path is relative to the mount point, so leia.mov means /data/leia.mov.

fs ls
fs df
fs stat leia.mjpeg.mov
fs mkdir clips
fs rm old.mov
fs mv a.mov b.mov
fs cat notes.txt
fs hexdump leia.mjpeg.mov
fs sha256 leia.mjpeg.mov
fs bench

fs df reports how much of the volume is used; fs bench measures read and write throughput, which is worth running once if playback is stuttering.

items.title: In the browser
items.text:
In desktop Chrome, Edge or Opera, this is the board's volume, live. Upload by dropping files on the list, and play, show, download, rename or delete what is there. It is the same file manager as on The board in the browser, and it checks every transfer the same way fs_xfer.py does.

Managing the files from this page needs desktop Chrome, Edge or Opera, and JavaScript. Every other browser can use fs_xfer.py, described next.

items.title: From the host
items.text:
fs put and fs get move bytes over the console itself, using XMODEM-1K. You could drive them by hand, but the host-side tool does the framing, the baud switching and the verification:

python external/esp-console-kit/tools/fs_xfer.py -p /dev/cu.wchusbserial… put ~/clips/*.mov

Only one program can hold the serial port

Close idf.py monitor first. This is the single most common reason the tool appears to hang.

Other subcommands:

fs_xfer.py put -f --to clips data/leia.mjpeg.mov   # replace, into a directory on the board
fs_xfer.py get leia.mjpeg.mov /tmp/leia.mov        # download
fs_xfer.py sha256 leia.mjpeg.mov                   # hash it on the board
fs_xfer.py run "fs ls" "fs df"                     # run any console command

-f replaces a file that already exists; without it, an existing name is an error rather than a silent overwrite. Uploads land as <path>.part and are renamed into place only once complete, so an interrupted transfer cannot be mistaken for a good file.

items.title: Verification
items.text: put sends each file's length up front, so the board stores exactly that many bytes — plain XMODEM would otherwise pad the last block out with padding bytes. It then checks the SHA-256 twice: once against the bytes the board received, and once against the file read back from flash. A clip that passes both is byte-identical to the one on your disk.

items.title: Speed
items.text:
Direction Baud Measured Upload 460800 21 KB/s on a 100 KB file; 7–10 KB/s on 1.6–1.9 MB clips (2.5–4.5 minutes each) Download 230400 about 21 KB/s

The console returns to 115200 afterwards.

Those rates are a property of the host, not the protocol. They were measured on macOS with the CH343P bridge and WCH's CH34x driver, where writing a whole 1029-byte block in one go loses data between the driver and the bridge at 460800 and above; the tool works around it by draining each 512-byte piece, which costs about 35 ms a call. Raising the rate therefore does not help — 921600 managed only 7.5 KB/s. In the other direction, data coming from the board above 230400 loses bytes whatever the block size, which is why downloads are slower than uploads.

On another host, try higher rates with --xfer-baud and --get-baud.

On macOS, upload through cu.wchusbserial…

macOS lists the board twice. Through Apple's own driver (cu.usbmodem…), every 1 KB XMODEM block reaches the board with its data changed, so fs_xfer.py put fails on its first block. Downloads and the console work through either. The browser's file manager copes: it switches to 128-byte blocks, which arrive intact, at a small cost in speed.

items.title: The holoprojector
items.text:
Two servos aim the holo — pan for left and right, tilt for up and down — and the shared holo engine moves them the way a dome's basic holoprojectors move. For getting them connected, see Wiring the servos.

This board has exactly one holo, named holo, so its name can be left out of every command: holo wag rather than holo holo wag.

holo            # status: the light, the current motion, and both axes
holo help       # every verb and its options

The status, partway through a holo wag:

holo   horizontal pan, vertical tilt, light none
       motion wag, at x +27% y +0%
       h      pan     closed 1150 open 1900 us, at 1627 us (default range, not saved)
       v      tilt    closed 1300 open 1950 us, at 1625 us (default range, not saved)
  • motion is what is running and where the holo points, as x and y in −100…100%. Before anything has moved it reads position unknown.
  • Each axis line gives the servo, its endpoints and where it is now, or not moved since boot. An axis released with holo off adds limp. (default range, not saved) means it has never been calibrated (see below).
  • light is none on this board: the engine supports an LED (see The light), but none is configured.
  • When a motion is cut short because an axis refused it, the motion line ends with which motion, how long ago and why -- ; <motion> stopped <n> s ago: <reason>, the reason being not fitted or uncalibrated -- followed by the axis in brackets when one axis refused it. A holo stop or holo off is not a refusal and adds nothing.

items.title: Motions
items.text:
Verb Does holo center Both axes to the middle holo move <x> <y> To a point; x and y are −100…100, the percentage of the way from centre to an endpoint. + is right and up holo nudge <dx> <dy> The same, relative to where it is now holo twitch Random glances, until stopped holo wag Side to side, and back holo nod Up and down, and back holo scan A slow sweep, until stopped holo circle Round and back holo stop Motion stops where it is holo off Stop, and both axes go limp

Options, depending on the verb: -d <ms> how long a move takes, -r <pct> how far it ranges, -n <cycles> how many times, -p <ms> the period of a cycle, -t <s> how long to keep going, and -i <s-s> the interval between twitches.

holo wag -n 3 -r 60
holo scan -p 4000 -t 30
holo twitch -i 2-8

items.title: Going limp
items.text:
The servos are not driven at boot and stay limp until something moves them. holo off, or servo_off all, releases them again; the next move picks up from wherever they were left.

Leaving a servo driven against a hard stop will cook it, so holo off is the right way to finish.

items.title: Calibrating the travel
items.text:
Each axis has a working range in microseconds, defaulting to the range the original sketch used — 1150–1900 µs and 1300–1950 µs — inside an absolute 1000–2000 µs limit no servo is driven outside.

holo endpoints h 1150 1900     # pan: closed (full left), then open (full right)
holo endpoints v 1950 1300     # tilt reversed: closed above open turns the axis round
holo endpoints v clear         # back to the default travel

h is the horizontal axis and v the vertical. The first number is CLOSED — full left or full down — and the second is OPEN. Putting closed above open reverses the axis, which is the fix when one runs backwards.

Endpoints are saved in NVS under the pin (gpio17, gpio18), not the axis name, so they follow the wiring rather than the configuration. servo_list -o wide shows each servo's absolute and working ranges.

Motion works before you calibrate anything

The holo engine normally refuses to move until both axes have saved endpoints. This board opts out, because the defaults compiled in are the servos' real travel rather than a guess. Calibrate when your mount needs different limits, not to get started.

items.title: The individual servos
items.text:
The servo_* commands reach the two servos one at a time, in raw microseconds rather than percentages — useful for finding the endpoints to save.

servo_list -o wide
servo_move pan 1500
servo_sweep pan -t 5
servo_config pan 1150 1900
servo_off all

servo_register re-attaches both servos; it is harmless to run, since a pin already attached is left alone.

items.title: The light
items.text:
The holo engine also supports a light, with holo led and holo leia.

There is no light on this board

This firmware registers the holo with no light attached, so holo led and the light half of holo leia do nothing here. holo leia still centres and moves the axes. The NeoPixel ring is driven separately by leds, and is not wired to the holo engine. Over Cyphal the ring is the holo's light: r2.holo.Light sets it with the same modes, a leia included (the holo on Cyphal), and leds has them too (the holo's light).

items.title: The host link
items.text:
What's in the firmware so far

UART and RS485, with JSON lines, native frames and events, and CAN, which hands the pins to the Cyphal node. I2C is described here ahead of the firmware. RS485 has been tried through a plain UART, not yet with a transceiver.

The host link lets another controller run the board over a wire: an Arduino or MarcDuino, a dome controller, another ESP32, or a Raspberry Pi. It plays scenes, shows clips, sets the LEDs and moves the holo, and hears back when a clip or scene has ended.

It uses three spare pins on the P2 header, and doesn't touch the USB console or Wi-Fi: all three work at once.

items.title: Choosing a transport
Pins
items.text:
Role Default P2 pin UART RS485 I2C CAN A GPIO21 11 TX (board → host) DI of the transceiver SDA TXD of the transceiver B GPIO33 12 RX (host → board) RO of the transceiver SCL RXD of the transceiver C GPIO15 7 ATTN, if turned on DE and /RE of the transceiver IRQ (open drain) not used

A GND wire, P2 pin 1 or 5, goes with every transport. The pins can be changed in the settings, to any of the free GPIOs that the LEDs and servos aren't using. While the link holds a pin, the gpio command refuses to drive it, and says what has it:

gpio 21 is reserved: CAN TX, for the Cyphal node (`link mode can`)

If the transport doesn't start, the link holds no pins, and link says so.

Everything is 3.3 V, and no pin takes 5 V. Each transport's page says what to put between the board and a 5 V host.

items.title: Turning it on
items.text:
The link is off until it's given a transport. The settings are saved, and can be changed from the USB console, the HTTP API, or the web app.

On the console:

link mode uart -b 115200
restart

After the restart, link shows it running:

link: uart on GPIO21 (TX), GPIO33 (RX), 115200 baud, protocol auto, address 1
  requests 0, events given 0, bad lines 0, framing errors 0, overruns 0, ignored 0; last request never
  events: [], pushed, 0 pending

Over the HTTP API:

curl -X PATCH -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"mode":"uart","baud":115200}' http://holo-2db0.local/api/v1/link

In the web app: the Host link card on the Settings page.

On CAN the board runs no host protocol: the pins go to the Cyphal node, whose cyphal command reports on it. The protocol, baud rate, address, groups, reply delay and events are kept for UART and RS485, and can still be changed, but CAN doesn't use them: link and the web app leave them out while the link is on CAN, and the console says so when one is changed.

Changing the transport, the pins, attn, the I2C address or general_call waits for a restart, and the reply says so with "restart_required": true. The rest applies at once: the baud rate, the address and groups, the protocol, and the events it starts with. A new baud rate takes effect after the reply, which is sent at the old one.

items.title: The link command
items.text: Command Does link The transport, its pins and settings, the counters, and the events asked for. On CAN, the pins and who has them link mode <off\|uart\|rs485\|can> [-b <baud>] [-a <address>] The transport, from the next restart. -b is the baud rate, -a the board's address: 1–223. can hands the pins to the Cyphal node link proto <auto\|json\|native> What the board accepts on UART and RS485. I2C is always native link address <1-223> The board's address on UART and RS485 link groups [<group>…\|--clear] The groups it belongs to, 1–31, up to 8 link pins <a> <b> <c> The GPIOs for roles A, B and C link events [<kind>…\|--none] [--push\|--keep] The events the link starts with, and whether it pushes them link log [on\|off] Print every line and frame, in and out, on the USB console. For wiring up a host link reset Back to the firmware's defaults

items.title: What a host can do
items.text:
Over JSON lines, most of the HTTP API: the screen, the LEDs, the holo and servos, scenes, settings, the board's information, and the link itself. The protocol reference lists the paths. Files, firmware updates, the network and servo calibration stay on the USB console and Wi-Fi.

Over native frames, less, but what a show needs: apply a scene by its slot, end it, the screen's colour and backlight, the LEDs, a holo motion, and the board's status.

Scenes do the heavy lifting. Set up the scenes on the web app, give each one a slot, and a host needs only "scene 3" to change what the screen, the LEDs and the holo are all doing.

items.title: Events
items.text:
A host can hear about things as they happen, rather than asking. They are the board's own events, the same ones the web app follows:

  • what happened: clip_started, clip_ended, scene_started, scene_ended, and touch (when touch reporting is on);
  • what changed: screen, leds, holo, scene, scenes, settings, network, ota and system, each with the resource as its GET returns it;
  • ready: the link has started (always sent once on UART, after a restart).

Nothing but ready is sent until the host asks, with PATCH /link/events or the native EVENTS_SET. On UART, the board sends events as they happen, with no extra wire. On RS485 and I2C, the host fetches what happened, and every reply says how many are waiting. Events has the details.

items.title: Status
items.text:
link on the console, and GET /api/v1/link, count what the link has seen:

Counter Counts requests Requests answered events Events given to the host bad_lines JSON lines that didn't parse, or were too long crc_errors Native frames dropped for a bad CRC framing_errors Bytes the UART received damaged: usually a wrong baud rate, or noise overruns Bytes lost because the host sent faster than the board read ignored RS485 lines with no address

A host that gets no reply at all is usually a wiring or baud-rate problem: link log on shows whether anything arrives. Each transport's page has a first test to try.

items.title: Images
items.text:
image show puts a PNG, a baseline JPEG or a GIF from /data in the middle of the round panel, where it stays until something else takes the screen. A still has no task and no timing behind it: it is drawn once and then simply left, exactly as a colour is. An animated GIF plays — see Animated GIFs.

For clips, see Video clips.

items.title: Preparing a file
items.text:
The panel is 240×240, and an image has to fit it — anything larger is refused rather than scaled or cropped, so the framing stays yours. Resize on the host:

sips -z 240 240 <input> --out r2.png            # macOS, built in
ffmpeg -i <input> -vf scale=240:240 r2.png      # anywhere

Smaller images are centred, with the rest of the panel black.

A JPEG has to be baseline and 4:2:0

The decoder reads baseline JPEG at 4:2:0 chroma subsampling. Two things it will not read, and what each reports:

The file is image show says Progressive only baseline JPEG is supported 4:4:4 unsupported colour sampling; re-encode as 4:2:0 4:2:2 bad JPEG data: corrupt, or colour sampling the decoder cannot read

This catches people out because ffmpeg picks 4:4:4 by default when the input is a still RGB image — unlike a clip, where the input is already 4:2:0. Ask for it explicitly:

ffmpeg -i <input> -c:v mjpeg -q:v 3 -pix_fmt yuvj420p r2.jpg

PNG is far more forgiving: palette, greyscale, grey+alpha, RGB and RGBA, at 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 bits, interlaced or not, all decode. Unless you have a reason to send a JPEG, send a PNG.

Transparency is composited over black, which is what the panel wakes to — so a transparent background comes out the same as a black one, not white.

A file that was truncated in transfer is refused rather than half-drawn, with libpng's own reason: image: /data/r2.png: Read Error.

Put the file on the board with fs_xfer.py put, then show it.

items.title: Showing
items.text:
image show r2.png
image show leia.jpg

Each reports what it did:

image: showing /data/r2.png (240x240 PNG, 16-line blocks, 118.4 ms)

The image stays until a clip, a colour, the calibration pattern or another image replaces it. screen reports it while it is up, and screen clear takes it away and puts the panel back to sleep.

screen

showing /data/r2.png (240x240, backlight 100%)

Nothing that fails ever disturbs the screen. The file, its format and its size are all checked before the panel is touched, so a rejected image show leaves whatever was already showing in place.

items.title: Animated GIFs
items.text:
A GIF with more than one frame plays, on its own frame delays, the same way a clip plays on its own timing:

image show r2-wave.gif

image: playing /data/r2-wave.gif (240x240 GIF, 24 frames, loops forever)

It loops the way the file says, which is how it looks in a browser: forever, a set number of times, or once if the file does not say. When a GIF that stops runs out of passes, its last frame stays up — it was shown as an image, and an image stays until something replaces it. screen says playing while it moves and showing once it has stopped.

It plays on the same task as clips, so everything that works on a clip works on a GIF: video stop stops it and puts the panel to sleep, video status reports its frame times, and another image, clip or colour replaces it without the panel blinking. A one-frame GIF is a still like any other.

A GIF that runs out of memory after it was accepted

A GIF takes its memory (its decoder and the buffers it paints from) only once what was playing has stopped and given back its own, so a full-width GIF replaces a playing clip or GIF like anything else. The other side of that: the file is checked before the show is accepted, but its memory is taken after, so if the board is short of internal RAM at that moment the show is still accepted (HTTP 200) and the animation ends at once. The console prints why once (out of memory for the decode buffers, say), clip_ended comes with finished: false, and the screen goes dark rather than keep what was there.

items.title: Making one
items.text:
From a clip or any video, at 240 pixels across and a frame rate the panel can keep up with:

ffmpeg -i <input> -vf "fps=15,scale=240:-1:flags=lanczos,split[a][b];[a]palettegen[p];[b][p]paletteuse" r2-wave.gif

The palette pair builds one 256-colour palette for the whole animation instead of a generic one; the difference is obvious. ffmpeg also writes each frame as only the rectangle that changed, which is what makes a GIF cheap to play here — see the table below.

Very short frame delays play at 100 ms

A frame with no delay, or a delay of 10 ms or less, stays up 100 ms. That is what Chrome and Firefox do, and files that ask for no delay were made expecting it — so a GIF runs at the speed it has in a browser, not faster.

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
Measured on the board with video status. What matters is how much of the picture changes from frame to frame, not how big the picture is: only the changed area is decoded and painted.

GIF Frame budget Decode + draw per frame Late ffmpeg, 240×240, 20 fps (a test pattern with moving parts) 50 ms 5.9 ms none ffmpeg, 120×120, 20 fps 50 ms 1.9 ms none Every pixel changing, flat colours, 240×240 — 30.7 ms — Every pixel changing, random noise, 240×240, 25 fps 40 ms 44.9 ms all

The last row is the ceiling: a 240×240 GIF that repaints the whole panel with incompressible content every frame manages about 22 fps. Real animations rarely come near it. If one stutters, video status will show frames running late; drop its frame rate, or its size.

items.title: Looking at a file
items.text:
image info r2.png

reports what the file contains without decoding it or touching the panel:

/data/r2.png: PNG 200x150, 8-bit RGBA, non-interlaced, 14233 bytes
parsed in 3.2 ms

For a GIF it counts the frames and adds up their delays, by the same rule it plays them:

/data/r2-wave.gif: GIF 240x240, 24 frames, loops forever, 1.60 s a pass, 412306 bytes

As with video info, it is the quickest way to find out whether a file survived its upload intact. A GIF cut short in transfer is refused outright — truncated: it ends before the GIF trailer — rather than played with its last frame half garbage.

items.title: How it is decoded
items.text:
PNG and JPEG end up in the same place: 16 lines at a time into one of two small DMA buffers, each block sent to the panel while the next is prepared. It is the mechanism the clip player uses, because a still has the same problem — a 240×240 frame is 115 KB, more than the largest free block of internal RAM.

Two things fall back to decoding the whole image first, and image show names which:

Case Mode reported The usual one 16-line blocks A JPEG whose width or height is not a multiple of 8 whole image An interlaced PNG whole image, in PSRAM

Adam7 interlacing cannot be read row by row: each of its seven passes writes only its own pixels into rows the later passes fill in, so every row has to be resident at once. That is 173 KB, which goes to PSRAM. A still has no frame to miss, so the slower path costs nothing but the wait.

A GIF is different, because its frames are rarely whole pictures: most are a rectangle drawn over the ones before. So it is composited onto a 240×240 canvas held in PSRAM, and then only what changed is sent, in the same 16-line blocks. video status calls this changed area only, from a PSRAM canvas.

items.title: What a still costs
items.text:
Measured on this board, from the command to the last pixel on the panel — decode, convert and paint together, which is what image show reports:

File Mode Time 240×240 PNG, RGB 16-line blocks 101 ms 240×240 PNG, RGBA 16-line blocks 107 ms 240×240 PNG, interlaced whole image, in PSRAM 175 ms 120×120 PNG, RGB 16-line blocks 40 ms 240×240 JPEG, 4:2:0 16-line blocks 27 ms 120×120 JPEG, 4:2:0 16-line blocks 17 ms

JPEG is three to four times quicker than PNG at the same size, which is the difference between a decoder written for this chip and a general-purpose one doing zlib on the CPU. Neither matters much for something shown once — but the very first image show after a restart takes about twice as long as the table says, while libpng and zlib claim their buffers for the first time.

Why it is built this way is in Video internals.

items.title: LED patterns
items.text: The leds command drives the NeoPixel ring: a solid colour, a pattern, or off. For getting the ring connected in the first place, see Wiring the LED ring.

items.title: What it is showing
items.text:
leds

reports the current mode and colour, whether a pattern is looping, a pulse's or a blink's period, a level other than 100 (see the holo's light), the brightness, a timed mode's time left and what follows it, and the hardware it is driving — how many LEDs, on which GPIO, at which data rate and in which colour order. That last part is the quickest way to confirm the strip is configured the way your hardware actually is.

items.title: A solid colour
items.text:
leds colour red
leds colour #ff8000
leds colour 255,128,0
leds colour 255 128 0

A colour is a name (red, orange, …), #RRGGBB or bare RRGGBB, or three decimal values either comma-separated or as separate words. color is accepted as well as colour.

leds off

turns the strip off; leds stop does the same thing.

items.title: Patterns
items.text:
Command Pattern leds wipe [<c>] [loop] Each LED to the colour in turn, 250 ms apart. White if no colour is given leds rainbow [loop] The colour wheel five times round the ring in 12.8 s, spread once round it and gamma-corrected

Each pattern plays once, holds for a second, and then turns the strip off. With loop it repeats until leds off.

leds wipe
leds wipe blue
leds wipe blue loop
leds rainbow loop

rainbow takes no colour — it is the whole wheel — so leds rainbow green is an error rather than a tint.

items.title: Flicker, pulse and blink
items.text:
leds flicker
leds flicker #4da6ff
leds pulse
leds pulse blue -p 3000
leds blink red -p 400

flicker makes the colour flicker like a failing hologram: mostly bright and restless, each LED a little apart from the others, with the odd dropout to near dark and a short stutter. pulse fades the colour up from dark and down again once a period (2 s unless -p gives another, 200–60000 ms), evenly to the eye. blink lights the colour for the first half of each period and turns it off for the second (1 s unless -p gives another). White if no colour is given. Unlike the wipe and the rainbow these have no end: each runs until something else takes the strip, such as leds off, another pattern, or a scene. Paired with a clip in a scene, a flicker makes the ring look like part of the hologram.

items.title: The holo's light
items.text:
The ring is also the holo's light: a controller on Cyphal sets it with the light modes a dome panel's own holos have. The same can be done here. Every mode but off takes a level, and colour, off, flicker, pulse and blink a time:

Option Does -l <pct> The level, 0–100: a share of the brightness this mode lights at. 100 unless given. 0 lights nothing. A wipe's or a rainbow's comes after its loop -t <s> For this long, 0.1–3600 s, and then back to what the ring was doing before: its mode, colour and level 
leds pulse orange -l 40
leds wipe blue loop -l 30
leds colour red -t 5
leds off -t 2

A timed mode during another timed mode goes back, when its time is up, to what the first would have gone back to, so a chain of them unwinds in one step. Any other leds command but bright, or a scene, during a timed mode replaces it for good. A wipe or a rainbow playing once goes back to off, where it would have ended by then. leds shows a timed mode with how long it has left and what follows:

solid #ff0000; brightness 30%; for 4.2 s more, then pulse #ffa500, every 2000 ms, at 40%; 16 LEDs on GPIO16, 800 kHz, GRB

The level is a share of the brightness rather than a brightness of its own, so that the light at full is the ring at the brightness it is set to (leds bright), never more: the limit below holds whatever a controller asks for.

items.title: Brightness
items.text:
leds bright 30

Brightness is a percentage from 1 to 100, applied to everything the strip shows, and it is the main thing standing between you and a brown-out.

30 is the ceiling on VSYS

Sixteen WS2812s at full white can draw about 1 A, which is more than the P2 header's contact and a shared USB supply can give. Powered from VSYS, keep leds bright at 30 or below. Full brightness needs the strip on its own 5 V supply — see the power section.

The boot brightness is set in menuconfig (LEDS_BRIGHTNESS, 100% by default); see Configuration.

items.title: Updating the firmware
items.text:
Once the board is installed, a new version of the firmware can go on in two ways, neither of which needs the board's buttons or its auto-reset circuit:

  • Over Wi-Fi, from a phone or a computer: the easy way once the board is on your network or you have joined its own access point.
  • Over serial, through the console on the USB-C port: when there is no Wi-Fi.

Either way the new image goes into the application slot that is not running, and the board checks the whole of it before it can boot. When it goes wrong, the image that was running still boots.

items.title: Updating over Wi-Fi
items.text:
Open the board's web app (see The board over Wi-Fi for how to reach it) and go to Update. There you can:

  • Install the latest release. The page shows the newest release next to what the board runs. Download and install has the board fetch the release from this site itself, checked against the release's SHA-256.
  • Upload a file. Choose holo-player-fw-vX.Y.Z.bin from a release, or build/holo-player-fw.bin from your own build. Before sending, the page reads the file and says which firmware and version it is. It warns about a downgrade, or about a file for another project. The bootloader and partition-table files from a release are not firmware, and the page says so.
  • Switch slots. The other slot still holds the previous firmware. Switch to this restarts into it.

After an upload or download, the new firmware is staged: checked and ready, but not yet what the board boots. Restart into it makes it the boot image and restarts. The page then waits for the board to come back and reports what it is running. Leave Restart into it once the board has checked it ticked, and an upload does all of this in one go.

A 1.6 MB image uploads in about 15 seconds over Wi-Fi, a third of the time it takes over serial.

items.title: From a script
items.text:
The web app is a front end for the board's HTTP API, so the same steps automate. Upload, activate and restart in one call:

curl -T build/holo-player-fw.bin "http://holo-2db0.local/api/v1/ota/image?activate=1&reboot=1"

Or have the board fetch the latest release, and install it only once it is staged:

curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"channel":"latest"}' http://holo-2db0.local/api/v1/ota/pull
curl http://holo-2db0.local/api/v1/ota/image          # until "state" is "staged"
curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{}' http://holo-2db0.local/api/v1/ota/activate

items.title: From the console
items.text:
The board can fetch an update from its console too: a release channel, a release's manifest, or an image's URL. It downloads the image, checks it, makes it the boot image and restarts, as ota put does:

ota pull latest
Flag Does -s Stage it only; ota activate makes it the boot image later -n Make it the boot image, but do not restart -f Accept an image built for another project --sha256 <hex> Refuse the image unless it has this SHA-256

ota activate makes the staged image the boot image and restarts. ota activate ota_1 does the same for the image already in a slot, which is how to go back to the firmware before.

items.title: Updating over serial
items.text:
Installing over USB needs the USB-C port and its auto-reset circuit. Once the board is mounted inside a droid that may not be reachable, so the firmware can also replace itself through the console it is already talking on.

python external/esp-console-kit/tools/fs_xfer.py -p <port> ota build/holo-player-fw.bin

A 1.26 MB image takes about 44 seconds. As with any host-side tool here, close idf.py monitor first — only one program can hold the serial port.

items.title: What happens
items.text:
The flash carries two application slots, ota_0 and ota_1, of 2.25 MB each.

  1. The board erases the slot that is not running and receives the image over XMODEM-1K at 460800 baud, writing each block as it arrives.
  2. ESP-IDF checks the complete image — its header, that it was built for this chip, and its SHA-256 — before it is allowed to become the boot image.
  3. The board makes that slot the boot image and restarts into it.
  4. The tool waits for the console to come back and confirms that the new slot is the one running.

items.title: When it goes wrong
items.text: A failed transfer, a truncated image, or an image built for something else changes nothing: the image that was running still boots. There is no state in which the board is left with no working firmware, because the slot being written is never the slot being run.

items.title: Rollback
items.text:
CONFIG_BOOTLOADER_APP_ROLLBACK_ENABLE is on, so a newly installed image boots on trial. It confirms itself once the application is up and the console is running. A reset before that point boots the previous image instead.

Rollback lives in the bootloader

The trial-and-confirm logic is part of the bootloader, and the bootloader is only written by installing over USB — from the browser, with esptool, or with idf.py flash. A board that has never been installed over USB with this firmware does not have it.

items.title: Checking the slots
items.text:
ota

lists both application slots: the partition label, where it is, how big it is, which one is running and which boots next, and for each one the project name, version and build date of the image it holds, plus its state.

This is where the release version becomes visible on the board:

ota_0    0x010000  2304 KB  running, boots    holo-player-fw v0.1.0, built Sep 20 2026 14:02:11

An image built from an untagged tree reports the commit it came from instead of a tag. See RELEASING.md for how the version gets there.

items.title: Options
items.text:
ota put is the on-board half, and fs_xfer.py ota drives it. Driving it by hand:

ota put [-b baud] [-n] [-d] <size>
Flag Does -b <baud> Transfer at this rate instead of the default -n Make the image the boot image, but do not restart -d A link test: receive and hash the image, write nothing

-d is the useful one when a transfer is failing and you want to know whether the problem is the link or the flash. fs_xfer.py ota --dry-run does the same from the host.

items.title: Going back
items.text: Installing over USB always writes to ota_0 and boots it, whichever slot was running before — whether from the browser, with esptool, or with idf.py flash. That is the way back if an update leaves the board in a state you would rather leave behind.

items.title: Video clips
items.text:
The player reads Motion-JPEG QuickTime files from /data and draws them centred on the round panel, timed by the clip's own time-to-sample table — so a clip plays at the speed it was authored at, not at whatever rate the decoder happens to manage.

For a single picture, or an animated GIF, see Images. An animated GIF plays on the same task as a clip, so video stop and video status work on it too.

items.title: Making a clip
items.text:
Export at 120×120; anything up to 240×240 fits the panel. Then convert:

ffmpeg -i <input> -c:v mjpeg -q:v 9 -an <output>.mjpeg.mov

-q:v 9 trades quality for size, and -an drops the audio track, which the board has no use for.

Width and height must both be multiples of 8

JPEG is coded in 8×8 blocks, and the fast path decodes 16 lines at a time. A clip whose dimensions are not multiples of 8 still plays, but silently falls back to decoding whole frames, which is about twice as slow at 240×240. 120×120 and 240×240 are both fine; 150×150 is not.

Put it on the board with fs_xfer.py put, then play it.

items.title: Playing
items.text:
video play leia.mjpeg.mov
video play leia.mjpeg.mov loop
video stop

loop repeats the clip until video stop. Without it, the clip plays once and the screen turns off — the panel sleeps with its backlight off whenever nothing is showing.

Starting another clip, an image show or a screen colour over a playing clip keeps the panel on and swaps what is on it.

items.title: Looking at a clip
items.text:
video info leia.mjpeg.mov

reports what the file contains — dimensions, frame count, durations — without playing it. It is also the quickest way to find out whether a file survived its upload intact.

video status

reports, per frame: the time to read it from flash, to decode it, and to decode and draw it. It also reports the paint time, from the first pixels sent to the panel to the last. Paint time is what tearing depends on: it is how long the panel spends halfway through an update.

items.title: Decoding modes
items.text:
By default frames are streamed: decoded 16 lines at a time into one of two small DMA buffers, with each block sent to the panel while the next one decodes.

video play leia.mjpeg.mov frame

forces whole-frame mode, which decodes the entire frame before sending any of it. This is also the automatic fallback for clips whose dimensions are not multiples of 8.

To check the fast path against the slow one:

video verify leia.mjpeg.mov

decodes sample frames both ways and compares them byte for byte.

Measured on the test clips at 30 fps — a 33.3 ms frame budget:

Clip Streamed: decode+draw Streamed: paint Whole frame: decode+draw Whole frame: paint 120×120 4.6 ms 4.1 ms 4.9–5.2 ms 3.2 ms 240×240 14.2–14.6 ms, none late 13.6 ms 28.3–30.2 ms, some late 17.8 ms

Why streaming exists at all, and what the numbers mean, is in Video internals.

items.title: If a frame is late
items.text:
Anything that writes to flash while a clip plays — saving a Wi-Fi network, an NVS write — pauses both CPU cores for the duration of the write, and can make a frame late.

The firmware already handles the one case it controls: the console's command history is written only when no clip is playing. Everything else is up to you. If playback stutters in a way that video status says it should not, look for something writing to flash.

items.title: The board over Wi-Fi
items.text:
Once the board is on your Wi-Fi, it serves a web app. It works on a phone or a computer, with nothing to install. Everything the app does is an HTTP API call, so a script can do the same.

On a phone, Status, Show, Holo and Scenes are tabs along the bottom, and the other pages are under More. On a computer, the side bar lists them all.

Each page keeps up by itself. When the board changes, from the console, a script, a scene ending or another browser, every open page shows it at once. Up to three tabs follow the board this way; a fourth checks every few seconds instead.

Page What it does Status What the board is doing now, the firmware it runs, how it is connected, and whether a newer release is out Show What is on the screen, and its backlight. Play any clip or show any image on the board, show a colour or the alignment crosshair, or clear the screen. Set the LEDs' pattern, colour and brightness Holo Point the holoprojector by dragging on a pad, or start a behaviour: twitch, scan, wag, nod or circle. Calibrate each servo's travel, and set its drive policy Scenes Save what the screen, the LEDs and the holo do together, apply it with one tap, and choose the one the board starts with Files Browse the board's storage, upload clips and images (several at once, with progress), and rename, move, copy, download or delete them Settings What the board starts with (the scene, backlight, LED brightness and count, touch reporting), and the web app's name, password and trusted sites Network The Wi-Fi network the board is on, the ones it knows, what is in range, and its own access point Update Install new firmware from a file, or have the board fetch the latest release itself

items.title: Scenes
items.text:
A scene is what the screen shows, what the LEDs do and how the holo moves, saved together under a name. A scene can include any of the three parts. A scene with only the LEDs is an LED preset, and one with only a clip plays that clip.

To make one:

  1. On the Scenes page, choose New scene.
  2. Tick the parts it has. Fill from what's showing now copies whatever the board is doing now.
  3. Try it applies the scene without saving it. Save keeps it.

When it ends says what happens once the scene is over:

  • Leave it as it is: everything carries on as the scene left it.
  • Go back to before: the screen, the LEDs and the holo return to what they were doing before the scene. A twitching holo twitches again, and a looping clip plays again.
  • All off: the screen and LEDs go off, and the holo's servos go limp.

A scene ends when its clip has played (once, or its number of times), or after the seconds given, whichever is first, so "go back" and "all off" need a clip that doesn't play over and over, or seconds. While such a scene runs, the Scenes page shows it with End it now, which does what it would do at its end. Applying another scene, or showing something else in place of its clip, ends it without that.

Start with it makes the board apply that scene every time it starts. The board keeps 16 scenes. The console's scene command lists and applies them too: see Console commands.

items.title: Calibrating the holo
items.text:
The holo moves only within each servo's saved travel. To set the travel:

  1. On the Holo page, choose Calibrate on a servo.
  2. Move the slider until the holo is at full left (or, for tilt, full down), and choose Set the closed end here.
  3. Move it to full right (or up), and choose Set the open end here.
  4. Choose Save the travel. The board keeps it across restarts.

Forget it goes back to the firmware's default travel. The drive policy sets whether a servo keeps being driven once it has settled. Letting go at an end stops the buzz of a servo held against its stop.

items.title: On your network
items.text:
First, put the board on your Wi-Fi from its console. It remembers the network and rejoins it at every boot:

wifi_save <ssid> <passphrase>

(wifi auto off keeps the network but stops the rejoin at boot, for a board that should stay off it until asked; wifi auto on puts it back.)

Then ask the board where to find it:

web

web: on
  http://10.0.19.118/
  http://holo-2db0.local/
password: none: anyone on the network can update the board

Either address works:

  • http://holo-xxxx.local/: xxxx is the end of the board's MAC address, so each board has its own name. This works from macOS, iOS, Windows and Linux, and from most Android phones. To name the board yourself, use web hostname <name>.
  • The address itself: always works. Your router's device list shows it too, under the same name.

items.title: With no network: the board's own access point
items.text:
Out in the field, the board can be the network. It turns its own access point on by itself:

  • at start, when it can't join a network: none is saved, or the one it rejoins hasn't answered within 20 seconds;
  • when you press BOOT (the board's BOOT button, GPIO0, also on P2 pin 4) while it isn't on a network. It first tries the saved network again; if that hasn't worked 20 seconds later, the access point comes on. A press while it is already on starts its time over.

Either way, it turns off again after 5 minutes, whether or not anyone is on it. Meanwhile the board keeps trying its network. To keep the access point on, turn it on yourself: on the Network page, or on the console:

wifi ap on

I (59133) wifi_ap: access point holo-2db0 up at 192.168.4.1
ap: on, holo-2db0, channel 11, 0 clients
pass: taxg-kerx-k4cp
page: http://192.168.4.1/

Then:

  1. Join holo-xxxx from your phone or laptop with the passphrase shown.
  2. The phone offers to sign in to the network, which opens the board's page. If it doesn't, open http://192.168.4.1/.
  3. If the page opened in the phone's small sign-in window, open http://192.168.4.1/ in the real browser before uploading files. The sign-in window can't reliably pick files.

Keep these in mind:

  • The access point is off after every restart, including the restart that finishes an update, unless the board can't join its network then. Press BOOT, or run wifi ap on, to bring it back. While the board is on your network, the Network page turns it on and off too.
  • wifi ap says how long it has left (off in 4:25) when it came on by itself or from the button. wifi ap on keeps it on; wifi ap off turns it off now.
  • The passphrase is random. The board makes it the first time and keeps it. wifi ap shows it, and wifi ap --pass <passphrase> changes it. To change the network's name, use wifi ap --ssid <name>.
  • The station keeps working. If the board is also on your Wi-Fi, both addresses work at once. The access point then shares your network's channel.
  • The board has no internet on its own access point, so it can't fetch releases itself. The Update page offers to fetch the release on your phone and send it on instead. That works if the phone still has mobile data.

items.title: A password
items.text:
With no password, anyone on the same network can change, update or restart the board. On a network you share, set a password on the Settings page, or on the console:

web password <password>

Seeing what the board is doing stays open to everyone. Changes, downloading files, and the web settings now ask for the password. The web app asks for it once and keeps it until you close the tab. To remove it, run:

web password --clear

Even with no password set, a web page elsewhere can't drive the board from your browser. The board answers only requests that name it, and only in forms a browser won't send across sites, except for a few trusted sites. The HTTP API reference has the details.

items.title: Other sites and API tools
items.text:
Pages on a few trusted sites may call the board's API from your browser: Swagger Editor, and this project's astromech.co and davidiansmith.ca, with their subdomains. That is what lets the HTTP API explorer try requests on a real board. Every other site is refused. To see or change the list, use the Settings page, or run:

web cors

The HTTP API reference covers adding and removing sites. Set a password before you add a site you don't control.

items.title: Turning it off
items.text:
To stop the web server, run:

web off

The board remembers this across restarts. web on starts the server again.

items.title: Working on the web app
items.text:
The pages are in web/ in the repository. They are plain JavaScript modules and CSS, with no build step. The firmware build gzips them into the image. To try a change without rebuilding and reflashing, serve them from disk and pass the API through to a real board:

python tools/web_dev.py holo-2db0.local
# then open http://localhost:8080/

A new page is one module in web/pages/, listed in web/app.js. The page appears when the board's /api/v1/info lists its feature.
